sections.title: One provider, several operating surfaces
paragraphs: Claude can be used through conversational products, APIs, and coding-agent tools. These surfaces differ in authentication, billing, context packaging, tools, and operational control.
Choose the surface from the workflow: interactive thinking, application integration, or repository execution.

sections.title: Treat model details as volatile
paragraphs: Model names, context limits, pricing, and regional availability change. Link to current official documentation instead of embedding long-lived routing rules without a verification date.

sections.title: Match the product surface to the job
paragraphs: Conversational products support direct knowledge work, APIs integrate model behavior into software, and coding agents work across repositories and development tools.

sections.title: Applications need contracts
paragraphs: When software consumes model output, use structured contracts, validation, retries, and observable failure behavior instead of parsing unconstrained prose.

They always use unrelated providers
There is no practical difference

Use different model families when independent review matters.

sections.title: Start from the work
paragraphs: Evaluate providers against representative tasks, quality rubrics, latency, total cost, context needs, tool support, data controls, deployment requirements, and team operations.
A provider can be best for one workflow and a poor fit for another.

sections.title: Independence can improve review
paragraphs: For important review, a different model family can reduce correlated blind spots. Independence does not replace tests or expert judgment, but it adds a useful perspective.

Whichever provider was selected first
questions.explanation: Representative tasks and operational constraints measure fit for the actual workflow.

questions.prompt: Why use a different model family for important review?

To avoid writing tests
questions.explanation: Cross-family review adds independence but still requires objective checks.

modules.title: Design a Bounded Agent Loop
modules.summary: Turn a goal into an observable plan-act-check loop with explicit state, budgets, approvals, and stopping conditions.
objectives: Distinguish a fixed workflow from a model-directed agent loop.
Define loop state, observations, decisions, actions, and evidence.
Implement deterministic success, escalation, and budget-based stopping conditions.
Prevent untrusted observations from changing the agent's authority.

sections.title: A useful work order removes hidden decisions
paragraphs: Name the outcome, the files or systems in scope, the constraints, and what the agent must leave unchanged. Include the audience and why the result matters when those details affect implementation.
Define what proves completion: a test result, a rendered page, a source citation, a diff review, or another observable artifact.

code.label: Agent work order
code.code:
Outcome: [WHAT MUST BE TRUE]
Scope: [ALLOWED FILES OR SYSTEMS]
Trusted inputs: [SOURCES OF TRUTH]
Constraints: [MUST / MUST NOT]
Evidence: [TESTS, PREVIEW, OR REVIEW]
Stop when: [CONCRETE TERMINAL CONDITION]

sections.title: Treat retrieved material as data
paragraphs: Web pages, issue text, documents, logs, and tool output can contain instructions that conflict with the real task. Label them as untrusted data and keep authority in the work order.
When the task is ambiguous but low risk, the agent can make a documented assumption. When an assumption changes scope, permissions, cost, or external impact, it should stop for authorization.

sections.title: Make every loop transition observable
paragraphs: Represent the current objective, plan, completed actions, unresolved evidence, remaining budgets, and next allowed actions as explicit state. Each iteration should consume a trusted observation and produce one decision: act, finish, or escalate.

Do not use the model's prose claim of completion as the terminal signal. A deterministic controller should compare real evidence with the success contract and record why the loop continued or stopped.

code.label: Provider-neutral agent loop
code.code:
while budget.remaining > 0:
  observation = inspect_environment()
  decision = model.choose(allowed_actions, state, observation)
  if decision.kind == "finish" and verifier.accepts(state, observation): return COMPLETE
  if decision.kind == "escalate": return NEEDS_HUMAN
  result = execute_authorized(decision.action)
  state = record_transition(state, decision, result)
return BUDGET_EXHAUSTED

sections.title: Stop before uncertainty compounds
paragraphs: Bound iterations, wall-clock time, token use, spend, repeated failures, and identical actions. Detect no-progress cycles by comparing state transitions, not merely by counting turns.

A safe terminal state can be complete, needs-human, budget-exhausted, policy-blocked, or failed-with-recovery-evidence. Preserve enough state to resume deliberately without repeating a consequential action.
sections.callout: A loop that can only report success or keep going is not operationally safe.

modules.title: Design Typed Tool Contracts and Action Controls
modules.summary: Give an agent narrow, validated interfaces and enforce authority, idempotency, verification, and recovery outside the model.
objectives: Define typed tool inputs, outputs, errors, and side effects.
Validate model-selected arguments before executing application code.
Apply least privilege and exact-target approval to consequential actions.
Design idempotency, postcondition checks, and recovery for uncertain outcomes.

sections.title: Not every tool call carries the same risk
paragraphs: Reading a file, editing a local draft, sending a message, deploying production, and deleting data have different consequences. Permission design should reflect those differences instead of treating tool access as a single switch.
Prefer the smallest authority that can finish the task. Keep secrets out of prompts and logs, scope credentials to the required system, and expire temporary access.
sections.callout: Read-only inspection, reversible local change, external communication, production change, and destructive change each deserve a distinct policy.

sections.title: The schema is an API contract, not a permission grant
paragraphs: Give each tool one clear purpose and a narrow schema with required fields, enums, formats, length and numeric bounds, and additional properties disabled where the provider supports it. Validate again in application code because generated structure can still contain unauthorized or semantically unsafe values.

Return stable success and error shapes. Separate retriable transport failures from validation, authorization, policy, conflict, and unknown-outcome errors so the controller can make a bounded recovery decision.

sections.title: Approval belongs before the consequential step
paragraphs: A human gate is useful only when the reviewer can still prevent impact. Ask before sending, purchasing, publishing, deploying, or destroying, not after the action has already happened.
Safe automation also needs an idempotency strategy, a bounded retry policy, and a recovery path. Repeating a failed action blindly can duplicate messages, charges, or changes.

sections.title: Separate selection from execution
paragraphs: The model may select a tool and propose arguments. A trusted executor authenticates the caller, validates the schema, authorizes the resolved resource, binds any approval to that exact action, enforces limits, and only then calls the implementation.
Treat returned content as untrusted data. Verify the real postcondition and record a secret-safe audit event containing the request identity, decision, target, result, and recovery status.
sections.callout: Structured output improves parsing; it does not prove authorization, safety, or success.

modules.title: Operate, Recover, and Improve Agent Systems
modules.summary: Classify failures across the full agent stack, contain impact, reconcile uncertain actions, recover safely, and turn incidents into verified improvements.
objectives: Distinguish model, prompt, tool, retrieval, data, policy, orchestration, and infrastructure failures.
Triage severity and contain unsafe action, data exposure, cost, and cascading retries.
Recover with reconciliation, idempotency, rollback, replay, and human escalation.
Convert operational evidence into tests, controls, runbook updates, and measured improvement.

sections.title: Classify the failed boundary before changing the model
paragraphs: Model failures include unsupported or incorrect generation. Prompt failures encode ambiguous or conflicting behavior. Tool failures include bad contracts, authorization, execution, or postconditions. Retrieval and data failures include missing, stale, poisoned, malformed, or cross-tenant evidence.

Policy failures allow forbidden action or block required escalation. Orchestration failures misroute, loop, race, or lose state. Infrastructure failures include capacity, network, dependency, credential, storage, and deployment faults. Several classes can occur in one incident, so record evidence instead of forcing one convenient cause.

sections.title: Triage impact and contain first
paragraphs: Assess affected users, tenants, data, permissions, external actions, money, availability, and legal or safety obligations. Set severity from actual and credible potential impact, not from how fluent the agent output looks.

Contain by pausing the workflow or one tool, revoking credentials, disabling a route, reducing concurrency, switching to a safe fallback, or requiring manual approval. Preserve secret-safe traces, configuration versions, request IDs, and postcondition evidence before mutable state disappears.
sections.callout: When the real-world outcome is unknown, do not classify the action as failed and retry it blindly.

sections.title: Reconcile before retry, rollback, or replay
paragraphs: A transport timeout does not prove that a write failed. Query the system of record with an idempotency key or correlation ID, compare the intended and actual postcondition, then choose accept, compensate, retry, rollback, or escalate.

Retry only transient failures with exponential backoff, jitter, provider guidance, and a total budget. Do not retry validation, authorization, policy, or deterministic conflict failures unchanged. Roll back through a tested reversible path and verify the restored state.

code.label: Recovery decision
code.code:
if outcome == UNKNOWN: reconcile system_of_record
if unauthorized or policy_blocked: stop + escalate
if transient and retry_budget > 0: backoff + idempotent retry
if harmful change and rollback_tested: rollback + verify
otherwise: preserve evidence + human decision

sections.title: Give responders a decision-ready runbook
paragraphs: A runbook names triggers, severity, owner, communication channel, dashboards and queries, containment choices, credentials and approvals, reconciliation steps, rollback or fallback, validation, escalation, and closure criteria. Commands should be safe to copy and explicit about targets.

Status updates distinguish confirmed facts, hypotheses, actions, impact, and next decision. Notify affected people under the organization's incident and privacy obligations without exposing secrets or unsupported blame.

sections.title: Close only after recovery evidence and prevention work
paragraphs: Verify user-visible recovery, external postconditions, queues and retries, permissions, data isolation, cost, and monitoring. A green health endpoint alone may miss incomplete work or a duplicated side effect.

Write a blameless timeline and contributing factors, add the smallest reproducing case to the evaluation suite, improve the control at the failed boundary, rehearse the changed runbook, and measure recurrence. Track follow-up work to completion rather than treating the post-incident review as closure.

modules.title: Cost, capacity, and spend control for AI systems
modules.summary: This intermediate module teaches you to calculate unit cost, translate measured demand into capacity, forecast spend, and choose controls that balance financial limits with service reliability. After completing it, you can build and explain a provider-neutral cost and capacity plan instead of treating an invoice or budget as an unexplained total.
objectives: Calculate direct usage cost and cost per successful outcome from measured workload data.
Separate fixed, variable, shared, and avoidable costs so that a cost model does not hide important assumptions.
Calculate required capacity from peak demand, measured safe throughput, and an explicit headroom factor.
Forecast spend with documented workload and price assumptions while identifying environment-specific values as UNKNOWN.
Choose monitoring, alerting, budgeting, and enforcement controls appropriate to the consequence of exceeding a spend limit.
Explain how retries, rejected work, capacity headroom, and service objectives connect cost management to reliability.

sections.title: What this intermediate module assumes
paragraphs: This module is explicitly intermediate. It assumes that you can work with multiplication, division, percentages, averages, request rates, and basic monitoring concepts. It introduces the cost and capacity relationships needed here, so it does not assume prior knowledge of queueing theory, financial accounting, or any named provider.

Before this module, you may be able to read a usage total or budget. After it, you can turn measured demand, prices, successful outcomes, and load-test results into a documented cost and capacity plan. You can also distinguish an informative budget alert from a control that actually limits work.

Exact prices, billing units, discounts, quotas, and contract terms are environment-specific. They are UNKNOWN until established from the applicable agreement, rate schedule, and usage records. Do not substitute an example value for an unknown production value.

sections.title: Start with a measurable unit of work
paragraphs: A cost model needs a denominator. Depending on the system, useful denominators can include a request, completed document, resolved case, generated asset, evaluated candidate, or other outcome. The best denominator represents value delivered rather than activity alone.

Define a successful outcome before calculating unit cost. A request that failed, was rejected, timed out, produced an unusable result, or was discarded may still consume billable resources. Counting only submitted requests can therefore conceal the cost of unsuccessful work.

Use two related measures when possible. Direct usage cost per request equals direct usage spend divided by attempted requests. Total attributable cost per successful outcome equals all costs assigned to the workload divided by the number of successful outcomes. The second measure connects spend to delivered value, while the first helps diagnose technical consumption.

Record the measurement period, workload boundary, success definition, included cost categories, and allocation method beside each result. Without those definitions, two unit-cost figures can use the same label while measuring different things.

sections.title: Build a transparent cost model
paragraphs: Separate costs into categories before adding them. Variable costs change with measured usage. Fixed costs remain for the period even if workload volume changes within the relevant range. Shared costs support more than one workload and require a documented allocation rule. Avoidable costs are consumed without delivering the intended outcome, such as unnecessary duplicate work or repeated failed attempts.

For a simple usage tier with one rate, direct usage spend equals billable units divided by the rate denominator, multiplied by the rate. If different unit classes, tiers, or time periods have different rates, calculate each applicable segment separately and then add the results. A single blended rate is safe only when its derivation is documented and appropriate for the decision.

A practical period equation is: total attributable spend equals direct variable spend plus assigned fixed spend plus assigned shared spend plus other applicable charges or adjustments. Taxes, credits, discounts, and commitments must be handled according to the actual agreement. Their values and treatment are UNKNOWN when that agreement is not available.

Consider a hypothetical workload with 2,400,000 billable units in a period. The hypothetical rate is 0.24 currency units per 1,000 billable units, so direct usage spend is 2,400 times 0.24, or 576 currency units. If assigned fixed and shared costs total 192 currency units, total attributable spend is 768 currency units. If 100,000 attempts produce 96,000 successful outcomes, total attributable cost per successful outcome is 768 divided by 96,000, or 0.008 currency units. These numbers are teaching inputs, not market prices.

sections.title: Translate demand into capacity
paragraphs: Capacity is the amount of workload a system can handle while meeting its stated service objectives. A theoretical maximum is not the same as safe operating capacity. Safe throughput should be measured under representative conditions while observing latency, errors, and saturation. The monitoring guidance in the sources identifies latency, traffic, errors, and saturation as central signals.

For an online workload, choose a planning demand such as a measured peak request rate or a justified forecast. Measure the sustainable throughput of one deployable capacity unit under the required service objective. Then apply an explicit headroom factor for uncertainty and variation. Required capacity units equal the ceiling of planning demand multiplied by the headroom factor, divided by safe throughput per capacity unit.

Suppose a hypothetical workload has planning demand of 120 requests per second. Testing shows that one capacity unit safely handles 18 requests per second under the target latency and error conditions. With a headroom factor of 1.25, required capacity is the ceiling of 120 times 1.25 divided by 18. The result is the ceiling of 8.33, so the plan requires 9 capacity units.

Headroom is a stated risk choice, not free capacity. More headroom can improve tolerance for bursts or uncertainty but can increase provisioned cost. Less headroom can reduce provisioned cost but leaves less room for variation. Record why the factor was chosen and identify the condition that would trigger a revision.

Average demand alone is insufficient when demand varies materially. Review peaks, duration, request classes, latency distributions, errors, saturation, and backlog behavior. For batch work, the corresponding questions are how much work must finish, the completion deadline, and the measured amount of work each capacity unit completes within that interval.

sections.title: Forecast cost and capacity together
paragraphs: A spend forecast combines a workload forecast with the applicable cost model. Begin with workload drivers, convert them into attempted work and billable units, apply the relevant rates, and then add fixed and allocated shared costs. Keep the workload assumptions separate from price assumptions so that each can be changed independently.

Use scenarios when important inputs are uncertain. A lower, planning, and stress scenario can vary demand, success rate, retry rate, unit consumption, safe throughput, or price. Scenario labels do not make uncertain inputs factual. Mark an input UNKNOWN until measurement, a contract, or another authoritative record establishes it.

Capacity and spend forecasts must reconcile. If the capacity plan assumes nine continuously active units but the cost model includes only six, the models describe different systems. If the financial plan assumes demand will be rejected after a threshold, the capacity and service plans must account for those rejected requests.

Reforecast when actual demand, success rate, unit consumption, throughput, or applicable rates depart materially from the assumptions. The threshold for materiality is organization-specific and is UNKNOWN unless a governing policy defines it.

sections.title: Use layered spend controls
paragraphs: Spend visibility is the first layer. Meter the billable quantities and connect them to a workload, environment, request class, and outcome where feasible. Reconcile operational measurements with billing records because the system's technical counters and the bill may use different boundaries or timing.

A budget is a financial plan. An alert reports that observed or forecast spend has crossed a chosen condition. Neither one necessarily prevents additional work. Treating an alert as a hard limit is a control-design error unless a separate enforcement mechanism is explicitly connected to it.

Guardrails can include review requirements, usage envelopes, concurrency limits, request admission rules, and limits by workload or tenant. Enforcement can reject, delay, queue, degrade, or stop work, so each enforcement action needs a defined reliability and user impact. The overload guidance in the sources explains why accepting work beyond safe capacity can harm a service and why overload responses need deliberate design.

Use a control ladder. First measure and attribute spend. Next forecast and compare it with an approved envelope. Then warn owners early enough to act. Finally, enforce a limit only where the consequence of continued spending is greater than the consequence of delaying or rejecting work. Assign an owner, response time, escalation path, and recovery procedure to every alert or enforcement control.

Governance should make decisions traceable. Record the metric, threshold, scope, owner, intended action, exceptions, and review date. The risk-management source supports explicit governance, measurement, and management rather than relying on an undocumented control.

sections.title: Diagnose variance instead of guessing
paragraphs: When spend differs from plan, decompose the difference. Check workload volume, billable units per attempt, success rate, repeated attempts, capacity hours, allocation changes, applicable rates, fixed charges, credits, and timing. This turns a total variance into candidate causes that can be tested.

For example, spend can rise while successful outcomes remain flat if attempts increase but success rate falls. Cost per attempt may appear stable even though cost per successful outcome becomes worse. Looking at both measures reveals the difference.

Do not label a cost as waste solely because it did not produce an immediate successful outcome. Testing, safety checks, resilience capacity, and evaluation can be intentional. Classify a cost as avoidable only after comparing it with the workload's documented purpose and risk requirements.

Close the loop after a change. Verify whether spend, successful outcomes, latency, errors, and saturation moved as expected. A change that lowers unit cost but violates a service or quality objective is not an unconditional improvement.

sections.title: Run a repeatable operating review
paragraphs: A useful review begins with definitions: the workload boundary, successful outcome, service objective, measurement period, and cost categories. It then compares actual demand, capacity, spend, and unit cost with the plan. Variances are assigned to named causes only when evidence supports them.

The review should identify unknowns explicitly. Examples include an unconfirmed future rate, an unmeasured safe throughput, or an undocumented allocation rule. For each unknown, record what evidence would establish it, such as an applicable rate schedule, a representative load test, or an approved accounting policy.

Finish with decisions and verification dates. Typical decisions include revising the forecast, measuring a missing input, changing capacity, reducing unsuccessful work, or adjusting a control threshold. Recheck both financial and service outcomes after implementation.

questions.prompt: In the module's hypothetical cost example, what is the total attributable cost per successful outcome?
choices: 0.006 currency units
0.008 currency units
0.024 currency units
0.24 currency units
questions.explanation: Total attributable spend is 768 currency units and there are 96,000 successful outcomes. Dividing 768 by 96,000 gives 0.008 currency units per successful outcome.

questions.prompt: Planning demand is 120 requests per second, the headroom factor is 1.25, and safe throughput is 18 requests per second per capacity unit. How many capacity units does the module's formula require?
questions.explanation: Multiply 120 by 1.25, divide by 18, and round up. The result is the ceiling of 8.33, which is 9 capacity units.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a budget alert is correct according to the module?
choices: It necessarily stops new work when the budget is reached.
It reports a condition but does not necessarily prevent more work.
It proves that all recorded spend is avoidable.
It replaces the need to measure billable quantities.
questions.explanation: A budget alert provides information. Preventing additional work requires a separately designed and connected enforcement mechanism.

questions.prompt: Which denominator best supports a value-oriented unit-cost measure?
choices: Successful outcomes
Calendar days regardless of workload
Attempted requests with success ignored
The number of monitoring charts
questions.explanation: Total attributable spend divided by successful outcomes connects cost to delivered value and exposes the effect of unsuccessful work.

questions.prompt: What should you do when the applicable production rate has not been established?
choices: Use the hypothetical rate as if it were contractual.
Choose a plausible market rate and present it as fact.
Mark the rate UNKNOWN until an applicable agreement or rate schedule establishes it.
Omit variable usage from every future cost model.
questions.explanation: The module requires environment-specific rates to be marked UNKNOWN until authoritative contractual or billing evidence establishes them.

modules.title: Agent evaluation and trajectory scoring
modules.summary: This intermediate module teaches you to design an agent evaluation that separates task outcomes from trajectory quality. After completing it, you can define a scoring rubric, calculate a normalized trajectory score, handle invalid trials, and interpret results without confusing plausible behavior with verified success.
objectives: Distinguish outcome evaluation from trajectory evaluation.
Represent an agent trajectory as an ordered record of observations, actions, responses, and state changes.
Define measurable success conditions before running an evaluation.
Build a weighted trajectory rubric with observable criteria and scoring anchors.
Calculate and interpret a normalized trajectory score.
Separate agent failures from invalid trials caused by the evaluation setup.
Report outcome, trajectory, efficiency, and validity results without collapsing them into a misleading single number.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes that you understand the basic agent loop in which an agent receives an observation, selects an action, receives a response from an environment, and continues until it stops or reaches a limit. No advanced statistics, programming framework, or provider-specific knowledge is required.

After this module, you will be able to move from an informal judgment such as the agent looked convincing to a reproducible evaluation plan. You will be able to specify what success means, record what happened during an attempt, score observable properties of that attempt, and explain the limits of the resulting scores.

sections.title: Define the evaluation unit
paragraphs: An agent evaluation begins with a task instance. A task instance contains an initial state, instructions, permitted interactions, constraints, and a success condition. The evaluation unit is one attempt by one agent configuration on one task instance under stated conditions.

Define the success condition before examining the attempt. A success condition should be testable from the final environment state or another independent artifact whenever possible. For example, if the task is to change a stored record, success concerns the resulting record rather than an agent message claiming that the record was changed.

Also define termination conditions. An attempt can end because the task succeeds, the agent declares completion, a step or resource limit is reached, the environment rejects further interaction, or the evaluation infrastructure fails. These endings are not interchangeable and should be recorded separately.
sections.callout: A fluent final answer is evidence about what the agent said. It is not, by itself, evidence that the environment reached the required state.

sections.title: Represent the trajectory
paragraphs: A trajectory is the ordered record of an attempt. For this module, each step contains the observation available to the agent, the action selected by the agent, the environment response, and any observable state change. The complete record also includes the initial state, the terminal state, the termination reason, and resource measurements collected under the evaluation rules.

Order matters. An action can be reasonable after one observation but unsupported before that observation. A trajectory record therefore needs stable step ordering and enough information to connect each action to the evidence available at that point.

Keep observed data separate from evaluator interpretation. The action and environment response are observations. Labels such as unnecessary, unsafe, or well justified are evaluator judgments. Preserving this distinction makes disagreements easier to inspect.

Some agent designs expose intermediate reasoning, while others do not. Evaluation should not require private reasoning that is unavailable. Observable actions, responses, state changes, and final artifacts can still be evaluated consistently.

sections.title: Separate outcome and trajectory quality
paragraphs: Outcome evaluation asks whether the required result was achieved. A binary outcome records success or failure according to the predefined verifier. Across valid trials, success rate is the number of successful trials divided by the number of valid trials.

Trajectory evaluation asks how the agent proceeded. It can measure whether actions were relevant, whether required evidence was gathered before consequential actions, whether constraints were respected, whether repeated or ineffective actions occurred, and whether the agent stopped appropriately.

Outcome and trajectory scores answer different questions. A successful outcome can follow a poor trajectory, such as one containing unnecessary risky actions. A strong-looking trajectory can still end in failure. Report both rather than treating one as a substitute for the other.

Efficiency measures such as step count, elapsed time, or consumed resources are also distinct. Lower use is not automatically better because an agent can appear efficient by stopping before completing the task. Compare efficiency among attempts with the same evaluation conditions, and interpret it alongside success.

sections.title: Write the success contract
paragraphs: A success contract states what the evaluator will inspect and how it will decide success. It should identify the target state or artifact, required constraints, allowed tolerances if any, and the point at which verification occurs.

Prefer direct verification. If the task changes an environment, inspect the environment. If it produces a structured artifact, validate that artifact against the task requirements. Use a human or language-model judgment only when the criterion genuinely requires interpretation, and give that judge explicit scoring anchors.

Do not create or revise success rules after seeing which attempts would pass. That makes results depend on the evaluated outputs. If a defect in the contract is discovered, document the revision and rerun affected attempts under the revised rule.

sections.title: Build a trajectory rubric
paragraphs: A trajectory rubric converts observable properties into scores. Each criterion needs a name, a description of the evidence to inspect, and anchors explaining what each score means. Criteria should be sufficiently distinct that the same behavior is not rewarded or penalized repeatedly under different labels.

One suitable three-point scale is 0 for a clear failure of the criterion, 1 for partial or inconsistent satisfaction, and 2 for full satisfaction. This is a rubric definition, not a universal scale. An evaluation may use another scale if its anchors are explicit.

Possible criteria include action relevance, evidence use, constraint compliance, recovery after an error, and termination quality. Use only criteria that apply to the task and can be judged from the recorded trajectory. Do not score hidden intent.

A criterion called evidence use might assign 0 when a consequential action contradicts or lacks required evidence, 1 when some relevant evidence is gathered but important support is missing, and 2 when the required evidence is gathered and used before the action. These anchors tell evaluators what observations distinguish the scores.

Weights express the evaluation's declared priorities. Set them before scoring attempts. A critical constraint can also be handled as a separate pass or fail gate rather than allowing strong performance elsewhere to cancel its violation.

sections.title: Calculate the trajectory score
paragraphs: For criterion i, let s_i be the assigned score and w_i be its positive weight. The weighted mean is the sum of w_i times s_i divided by the sum of w_i. If every criterion uses the 0 to 2 scale, the weighted mean also ranges from 0 to 2.

To express that result on a 0 to 100 scale, divide the weighted mean by 2 and multiply by 100. For example, consider two criteria with weights 2 and 1. If their scores are 1 and 2, the weighted mean is ((2 times 1) plus (1 times 2)) divided by 3, which equals 4 divided by 3. The normalized trajectory score is (4 divided by 3) divided by 2, multiplied by 100, or approximately 66.7.

A normalized score is meaningful only in relation to its rubric. It does not establish that two evaluations measured the same construct merely because both report numbers from 0 to 100. Publish the criteria, anchors, weights, and aggregation rule with the score.
Keep hard failures visible. If violating a required constraint causes automatic failure, report that rule separately and do not hide the violation inside an average.

sections.title: Improve scoring consistency
paragraphs: Test the rubric on a small set of representative trajectories before using it for the full evaluation. Have evaluators identify which recorded evidence supports each score. Disagreement can reveal ambiguous anchors, missing trajectory data, or criteria that combine multiple ideas.

When human judgment is required, evaluators should use the same instructions and should not infer facts absent from the record. When a language model assigns scores, treat it as an evaluator with its own possible inconsistencies rather than as an unquestionable reference. The cited research on language-model judging documents the use and study of such evaluators, which supports checking their behavior rather than assuming perfect judgment.

For subjective criteria, retain the evaluator's criterion-level scores and concise evidence references. A single total score makes it difficult to discover whether disagreement came from evidence use, constraint compliance, or another criterion.

If the rubric or evaluator instructions change, preserve the revision and identify which attempts were scored under it. Comparing scores produced by materially different rules requires explicit qualification.

sections.title: Handle invalid trials and uncertainty
paragraphs: An invalid trial is one in which the planned evaluation was not actually conducted, such as when required task data is unavailable or the evaluation infrastructure prevents interaction. An agent failure is a valid trial in which the agent does not satisfy the task. Misclassifying difficult failures as invalid can inflate reported performance.

Define invalidation and retry rules before running the evaluation. Record the original attempt, the invalidation reason, whether a retry occurred, and which attempt entered the reported result. Do not silently remove trials.

If the available trajectory does not contain enough evidence to score a criterion, record that criterion as UNKNOWN rather than guessing. The aggregation rule must state how UNKNOWN values are handled. One defensible approach is to report coverage and avoid calculating a total score when a required criterion is unknown.

Missing evidence is not automatically evidence of failure unless the rubric explicitly requires the evidence to be present. For example, if the agent must verify a state before acting, absence of a recorded verification can legitimately fail the evidence-use criterion. Otherwise, the evaluator should not invent what happened.

sections.title: Report results without hiding tradeoffs
paragraphs: A useful report identifies the task set, evaluation unit, success contract, termination rules, invalid-trial policy, trajectory schema, rubric, criterion weights, aggregation rule, and evaluation conditions. It reports the number of valid, successful, failed, invalid, and UNKNOWN-scored trials rather than presenting only a percentage.

Present outcome success, critical constraint violations, criterion-level trajectory scores, total trajectory scores, and efficiency measures as separate results. This allows a reader to distinguish an agent that often succeeds inefficiently from one that behaves neatly but rarely completes the task.

Inspect individual trajectories as well as aggregate results. Repeated failure patterns can reveal missing evidence gathering, ineffective retries, premature stopping, or exploitation of a weak verifier. Such patterns should motivate a clearly documented evaluation revision, followed by rescoring or rerunning as appropriate.

Interactive-agent benchmarks in the cited sources evaluate agents through actions and environment feedback rather than final text alone. Their task designs differ, so their reported results should not be treated as interchangeable. The transferable lesson is to align the verifier and trajectory record with the environment and task being evaluated.

sections.title: Apply the workflow
paragraphs: First, define each task instance and its independently testable success contract. Second, specify allowed actions, limits, termination reasons, invalidation rules, and retry rules. Third, record ordered trajectories with initial and terminal states.

Fourth, score the outcome using the predefined verifier. Fifth, score trajectory criteria using observable evidence and fixed anchors. Sixth, apply declared weights and gates without changing them after seeing results. Seventh, report validity, outcome, trajectory, and efficiency measures separately.

Finally, review disagreements and failure patterns. Revise a defective evaluator only with a documented reason, and rerun or rescore affected attempts. This workflow makes an agent evaluation inspectable and repeatable without pretending that one aggregate score captures every property of agent behavior.

questions.prompt: An agent states that it updated a record, but inspection shows that the record did not change. Under the module's outcome rule, what is the correct result?
choices: Success, because the final statement claimed completion
Failure, because the required environment state was not achieved
UNKNOWN, because final statements cannot be evaluated
Success if the trajectory was otherwise efficient
questions.explanation: Outcome success is determined by the predefined success contract and the resulting state or artifact, not by the agent's claim.

questions.prompt: Which item belongs in a trajectory step as observed data rather than evaluator interpretation?
choices: The action selected by the agent
A label saying the action was unnecessary
A judgment that the agent behaved safely
A conclusion that the reasoning was poor
questions.explanation: The selected action is part of the observed record. The other choices are evaluator judgments that should be stored separately from observations.

questions.prompt: Two trajectory criteria use a 0 to 2 scale. Their weights are 2 and 1, and their scores are 1 and 2. What normalized score does the module's formula produce?
choices: Approximately 66.7
Approximately 83.3
questions.explanation: The weighted mean is ((2 times 1) plus (1 times 2)) divided by 3, or 4 divided by 3. Dividing by the maximum score of 2 and multiplying by 100 gives approximately 66.7.

questions.prompt: Required task data is unavailable, so the agent cannot begin the planned interaction. How should the attempt be classified under the module's definitions?
choices: A successful trial
An agent failure
An invalid trial with a recorded reason
A perfect trajectory with no actions
questions.explanation: The planned evaluation was not conducted because required task data was unavailable. The attempt should be recorded as invalid according to predefined invalidation rules.

questions.prompt: A required trajectory criterion cannot be scored because the record lacks enough evidence. What should the evaluator do?
choices: Guess the most likely score
Assign the highest score
Record UNKNOWN and follow the declared aggregation rule
Delete the trial without recording it
questions.explanation: The module requires evaluators to record UNKNOWN rather than inventing evidence. It also recommends reporting coverage and avoiding a total when a required criterion is unknown.

questions.prompt: Why should outcome success and trajectory quality be reported separately?
choices: Because a good-looking trajectory always guarantees success
Because outcome and trajectory scores answer different questions
Because trajectory scoring replaces direct outcome verification
Because efficiency is identical to task success
questions.explanation: Outcome evaluation asks whether the required result was achieved, while trajectory evaluation asks how the agent proceeded. Either can be strong while the other is weak.

modules.title: AI for Executives, Leaders, and Decision Makers
modules.summary: This intermediate module enables leaders to evaluate proposed AI uses, assign decision rights, demand decision-relevant evidence, and establish monitoring and escalation rules. After completing it, learners can turn an AI proposal into a documented decision to proceed, revise, restrict, pause, or reject.
objectives: Classify an AI proposal by organizational impact, uncertainty, reversibility, and exposure.
Define accountable owners and decision rights for an AI use.
Request evidence that connects system performance to a specific organizational outcome and operating context.
Write approval conditions, monitoring measures, escalation thresholds, and stop conditions.
Distinguish responsibility that can be assigned to a provider from accountability that remains with the adopting organization.
Make and document a decision to proceed, revise, restrict, pause, or reject an AI proposal.

sections.title: Level and Scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes familiarity with ordinary organizational planning, budgeting, risk, and accountability, plus a basic understanding that AI systems produce outputs from data and instructions. It does not assume programming, model-building, statistical, or procurement expertise.

The executive task is not to determine whether AI is impressive in the abstract. It is to decide whether a defined use should be authorized under defined conditions. A complete decision identifies the intended outcome, affected people, accountable owner, supporting evidence, permitted boundaries, monitoring measures, and conditions for escalation or stopping.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology organizes AI risk work around four functions: Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. Govern is cross-cutting, while the other functions address context, assessment, prioritization, and response. This module converts those functions into a practical leadership sequence rather than a technical implementation procedure.
sections.callout: Do not approve a general capability. Approve or reject a specific use, in a specific context, with a named owner and explicit conditions.

sections.title: Define the Decision Before Reviewing the Technology
paragraphs: Begin with a one-sentence decision statement: the organization is considering using an AI-enabled process to support a named task for named users in a named setting. State whether the output advises a person, prioritizes work, generates content, or directly triggers an action. This boundary prevents evidence about one use from being treated as proof for a different use.

Next, define the intended organizational outcome without referring to the AI itself. Examples include reducing unresolved requests, helping employees locate approved information, or improving the consistency of a review process. Then identify the present baseline. Without a baseline, a later change cannot be interpreted as improvement, deterioration, or no meaningful change.

Separate the output from the outcome. Producing a response is an output. Resolving a request correctly is an outcome. Classifying a case is an output. Making a timely and appropriate decision is an outcome. Executive evidence should connect output quality to the outcome that justified the proposal.

Identify who is affected, who operates the process, who can challenge an outcome, who can authorize changes, and who remains accountable. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development principles emphasize human rights, transparency, robustness, safety, and accountability. Those concerns require attention to people and operating context, not only to technical performance.

sections.title: Triage by Impact, Uncertainty, Reversibility, and Exposure
paragraphs: A practical portfolio triage uses four questions. Impact asks how serious a wrong or delayed outcome could be. Uncertainty asks how much relevant evidence is missing or how different the intended setting is from the tested setting. Reversibility asks whether an affected person and the organization can detect and correct an error. Exposure asks how many people, decisions, records, or business processes could be affected.

These dimensions guide the strength of review rather than producing an automatic score. A low-impact, reversible use with bounded exposure may justify a limited trial. A use with serious possible consequences, weak evidence, difficult correction, or broad exposure requires stronger review and controls. If the organization cannot describe the consequences or affected population, uncertainty remains unresolved and should not be silently treated as low risk.

Triage must consider the complete process. Human review does not by itself make a use safe or accountable. Leaders should ask whether reviewers have enough time, information, authority, and skill to detect and correct a problematic output. If they are expected merely to confirm it, the review control has not been demonstrated.

Record the reasoning behind the classification. The record should explain which consequences matter, what evidence is absent, how an error can be corrected, and what limits exposure. This allows a later reviewer to understand the decision instead of reconstructing it from memory.
sections.callout: High uncertainty is not evidence of high or low performance. It means the evidence is insufficient for the proposed decision.

sections.title: Assign Governance and Decision Rights
paragraphs: Name one accountable business owner for the use. That owner is responsible for the organizational outcome and for ensuring that approval conditions remain satisfied. Other roles may operate the process, assess evidence, protect information, review legal obligations, or respond to incidents, but distributing tasks does not eliminate the need for accountable ownership.

Define decision rights before deployment. Specify who may approve initial use, change its scope, accept a known limitation, pause operation, restore operation, and retire the use. Also specify who can receive and investigate challenges from affected people. Ambiguous decision rights delay action when conditions change.

Responsibility for supporting work may be assigned to an external provider, but the adopting organization still needs its own decision about the use. Provider evidence can inform that decision, yet it does not establish that the system is appropriate in every local workflow, population, or consequence setting.

The Govern function in the National Institute of Standards and Technology framework is cross-cutting. For leaders, this means accountability, policy, roles, risk tolerance, and oversight should shape mapping, measurement, and management rather than appearing only at the final approval meeting.

sections.title: Demand Decision-Relevant Evidence
paragraphs: Ask first what claim the evidence is meant to support. A useful claim names the task, population, operating conditions, outcome measure, and acceptable boundary. Evidence from a different task or setting may be informative, but its relevance must be explained rather than assumed.

Review evidence in four categories. Outcome evidence addresses whether the process achieves the intended result. Risk evidence addresses errors, harmful effects, security, privacy, and unequal effects on relevant groups. Operational evidence addresses whether people can use, supervise, challenge, and recover from the process. Economic evidence addresses the full organizational resources required to operate, review, correct, monitor, and retire the use.

For every measure, request a baseline, a decision threshold, a measurement method, a measurement frequency, an owner, and a predefined response. A measure without a threshold cannot by itself determine whether action is required. A threshold without an owner and response does not create an operating control.

Ask how testing represents the intended setting. Relevant questions include whether test cases cover ordinary and difficult conditions, whether affected groups are represented, whether reviewers used the same information and time constraints expected in operation, and whether failures were examined rather than averaged away.

Do not convert missing evidence into an unsupported claim. Record the item as UNKNOWN, identify what observation or test would establish it, and decide whether the unresolved uncertainty permits a bounded trial, requires more evidence, or prevents the proposed use.

sections.title: Set Boundaries, Controls, and Human Recourse
paragraphs: Approval conditions should state where the use is permitted and prohibited. Boundaries can cover eligible tasks, users, information, affected populations, output types, and actions that require independent authorization. A narrow boundary makes both evidence and accountability more specific.

Controls should address prevention, detection, response, and recovery. Prevention reduces the chance of an unacceptable event. Detection identifies when performance or operating conditions depart from expectations. Response assigns immediate action and communication. Recovery restores an acceptable process, corrects affected records or decisions where possible, and captures lessons for future decisions.

Provide a workable route for questions and challenges when people may be affected. The route should identify where a challenge goes, who reviews it, what information is available to the reviewer, and who can correct an outcome. Merely stating that a person remains involved does not establish meaningful recourse.

Document exceptions. If leaders accept a limitation, the record should state the reason, scope, duration, compensating control, accountable approver, and review date. An exception without an end or review condition can become an undocumented permanent policy.

sections.title: Choose and Document a Decision
paragraphs: A leadership decision can be to proceed, revise, restrict, pause, or reject. Proceed means the evidence and controls support the defined use. Revise means the proposal needs changes before authorization. Restrict means only a narrower use or population is authorized. Pause means a temporary stop is required while specified evidence or remediation is completed. Reject means the proposed use is not acceptable under the considered conditions.

The decision record should contain the use statement, intended outcome, baseline, affected parties, impact and uncertainty assessment, evidence reviewed, unresolved UNKNOWN items, accountable owner, decision rights, boundaries, controls, measures, thresholds, escalation path, stop conditions, review date, and final rationale.

A decision record should distinguish facts from judgments. Test results, incident records, and observed process measures are evidence. Risk tolerance and acceptance of a tradeoff are governance judgments. Both belong in the record, but presenting a judgment as if it were measured evidence prevents meaningful review.

Approval is not the end of governance. It is permission to operate while stated assumptions and conditions remain valid. A material change in purpose, population, workflow, information, consequences, or observed performance requires reassessment because the original evidence may no longer answer the same question.
sections.callout: An approval without boundaries, monitoring, and stop conditions is incomplete.

sections.title: Monitor Outcomes and Trigger Action
paragraphs: Monitoring should cover the intended outcome, known failure modes, operational behavior, challenges from affected people, incidents, corrective actions, and changes in context. Select measures because they inform a decision, not because they are easy to collect.

Each measure needs an action rule. A rule states what condition triggers investigation, restriction, pause, correction, or executive review. The threshold may be quantitative or qualitative, but it must be defined before the organization needs to rely on it.

Stop conditions identify circumstances in which continued operation is not authorized. Examples include loss of an essential control, evidence of a serious unaddressed effect, operation outside the approved boundary, inability to provide required review, or failure to produce required monitoring evidence. The accountable owner must know who can activate the stop and what process replaces the AI-enabled step.

Review dates are useful, but event-based review is also necessary. Reassessment should occur when the purpose, affected population, workflow, consequences, evidence, or operating environment changes materially. The decision record should state which changes count as review triggers.

After completing this module, a learner can take a proposal that previously consisted mainly of a capability description and convert it into an outcome-focused decision record with ownership, evidence requirements, boundaries, monitoring rules, escalation paths, and stop conditions.

questions.prompt: What should a leader define before deciding whether evidence supports an AI proposal?
choices: The broad capability that appears most impressive
The specific use, intended outcome, affected people, and operating context
A permanent approval date
A provider's preferred demonstration
questions.explanation: The module requires leaders to define a specific use, outcome, affected parties, and context before judging evidence. Evidence cannot be evaluated for relevance when the decision boundary is undefined.

questions.prompt: A proposed use has potentially serious consequences, limited relevant evidence, and errors that would be difficult to correct. Which response best follows the module's triage method?
choices: Treat it as low risk because no failure has yet been observed
Approve it because a person will be present somewhere in the process
Require stronger review and controls, and do not treat missing evidence as low risk
Ignore reversibility because only measured performance matters
questions.explanation: Serious impact, high uncertainty, and difficult reversibility require stronger review and controls. Missing evidence remains uncertainty and does not prove safety or performance.

questions.prompt: Which set of elements makes a monitoring measure usable as an operating control?
choices: A measure name and a presentation date
A favorable example and a general promise to review it
A baseline, threshold, method, frequency, owner, and predefined response
A provider description without a local outcome
questions.explanation: The module states that every measure needs a baseline, decision threshold, method, frequency, owner, and response. Together these elements connect observation to accountable action.

questions.prompt: What happens to organizational accountability when supporting work is assigned to an external provider?
choices: The adopting organization no longer needs an accountable owner
Accountability automatically transfers to the provider
The organization still needs its own accountable owner and decision about the use
Only the provider may pause the use
questions.explanation: Provider evidence and services can support a decision, but the adopting organization remains responsible for deciding whether the specific use is appropriate in its own context.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a stop condition?
choices: A circumstance in which continued operation is no longer authorized
A target that is reviewed only after retirement
A general preference for future improvement
A substitute for naming an accountable owner
questions.explanation: A stop condition defines when operation must cease, such as loss of an essential control or operation outside the approved boundary. It must be connected to authority and a replacement process.

modules.title: Fine-tuning, adapters, distillation, and when not to train
modules.summary: This intermediate module enables learners to distinguish full fine-tuning, adapter-based training, and distillation, then decide whether training is appropriate for a specific model requirement. After completing it, learners can select an approach, explain the trade-offs, and design a baseline evaluation before committing training resources.
objectives: Distinguish full fine-tuning, adapter-based training, and knowledge distillation by identifying what is trained in each approach.
Decide whether a requirement calls for behavioral adaptation, external knowledge retrieval, model compression, or no model training.
Choose an evaluation baseline and held-out checks before comparing a trained model with its starting model.
Identify data, governance, and operational questions that must be resolved before training.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes familiarity with training examples, model inference, and the distinction between training data and held-out evaluation data. It does not assume knowledge of optimization mathematics or any provider-specific training system.

In this module, fine-tuning means continuing training from an existing model by changing its trainable parameters for a target task or behavior. Full fine-tuning changes the original model parameters, while parameter-efficient approaches keep the original parameters fixed and train a smaller set of added or selected parameters. This distinction is described directly in the primary research on parameter-efficient transfer and low-rank adaptation [S1; S2].

sections.title: Start with the required change
paragraphs: Before selecting a training method, state the required change in observable terms. Examples include following a stable output format, applying a classification policy, answering from a changing document collection, or running a smaller model under a deployment constraint. This framing separates behavior changes, knowledge-access changes, and compression goals.

Do not begin with the assumption that training is required. Treat training as one possible intervention and compare it with simpler interventions that can satisfy the same acceptance test. If instructions or workflow controls already produce acceptable results, further training adds work without changing the decision outcome.

If the requirement is access to information that changes independently of the model, consider retrieval rather than encoding that information through training. Retrieval-augmented generation supplies retrieved text to a generator and was introduced as a way to combine learned model parameters with an external document index [S4].
sections.callout: Write the acceptance test before choosing the intervention. A method is suitable only if it improves the behavior that the test measures.

sections.title: Full fine-tuning
paragraphs: Full fine-tuning continues training while updating the original model parameters. The low-rank adaptation research contrasts this approach with freezing the original weights and training a much smaller set of added parameters [S2].

Consider full fine-tuning when the required behavioral change is broad enough to justify modifying the base model and when the team can evaluate, store, govern, and deploy the resulting model as a distinct trained artifact. This is a decision rule, not a guarantee that full fine-tuning will improve a particular task.

Do not infer success from training loss alone. Compare the resulting model with the unchanged baseline on held-out examples that represent the intended use, important failure cases, and unacceptable behavior. The evaluation should use the same tests for every candidate so that the intervention, rather than a changed test, explains the comparison.

sections.title: Adapter-based training
paragraphs: Classic adapter training inserts small trainable modules into a pretrained network while keeping the original network parameters fixed. The original adapter research demonstrated this structure as a parameter-efficient alternative to training a separate full model for every task [S1].

Low-rank adaptation also freezes the existing model weights, but it represents the trainable change through low-rank matrices associated with selected layers. Its primary paper describes this method as reducing the number of trainable parameters relative to full fine-tuning [S2].

Use adapter-based training as a candidate when you want a learned behavior change but also want to preserve an unchanged base model. Confirm that the intended training and serving environment supports the chosen adapter approach before designing around it. No universal compatibility claim is made here.

Adapter-based training is not automatically the best choice merely because it trains fewer parameters. The correct comparison is whether it meets the same held-out quality requirements and operational constraints as the alternatives.

sections.title: Knowledge distillation
paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a student model using a teacher model's outputs as part of the training signal. The foundational distillation paper describes training the student with softened teacher output distributions, optionally combined with the ordinary labeled objective [S3].

Distillation is therefore aimed at transferring behavior into a separate student, commonly when the desired outcome is a model that is easier to deploy under a size or computation constraint. The student must still be evaluated independently because it is a newly trained model rather than a reference to the teacher at inference time [S3].

Teacher outputs are training targets in the distillation process, so the evaluation must include cases where the teacher is weak or wrong. A student that closely imitates an unwanted teacher behavior has not met the deployment requirement, even if the imitation objective improved.

sections.title: How the approaches differ
paragraphs: The central distinction is what receives training updates. Full fine-tuning updates the original model parameters. Classic adapters keep those parameters fixed and train added modules. Low-rank adaptation keeps the original weights fixed and trains low-rank parameter changes. Distillation trains a separate student from a signal that includes teacher outputs [S1; S2; S3].

The approaches also answer different design questions. Fine-tuning and adapter-based training ask how to adapt an existing model's behavior. Distillation asks how to train a student to reproduce useful aspects of a teacher. Retrieval asks how to provide external information during generation without relying only on information encoded in model parameters [S4].
These categories can be combined in a larger system, but combination is not automatically beneficial. Each added intervention needs its own reason, acceptance test, and operational owner.

sections.title: When not to train
paragraphs: Do not train when the requirement is not yet testable. If stakeholders cannot provide representative inputs, expected outcomes, and unacceptable outcomes, there is no reliable basis for deciding whether training helped.

Do not train merely to insert frequently changing facts. A retrieval design can supply external passages during generation, allowing the information source to remain separate from the model parameters [S4]. Evaluate whether retrieved passages are relevant and whether generated answers are supported by those passages.

Do not train when a stable instruction, deterministic transformation, or workflow control already meets the acceptance test. In that case, training introduces another artifact to evaluate and govern without an established benefit.

Do not train on data whose permitted use, provenance, privacy requirements, or quality cannot be established. The risk-management framework published by the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology organizes AI risk work into Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage functions and treats documentation, measurement, and ongoing management as connected activities [S5].

No universal minimum training-set size is asserted in this module. The necessary amount and composition are UNKNOWN without a specified task, model, data distribution, target metric, and controlled evaluation.

sections.title: A practical decision procedure
paragraphs: First, define an observable target and a held-out evaluation. Record the unchanged model's results as the baseline. Include ordinary cases, difficult cases, and cases that must not produce the requested behavior.

Second, identify the change type. For a behavior change, test instructions or workflow controls before considering fine-tuning or adapters. For changing external knowledge, test retrieval. For a smaller student that should imitate a teacher, test distillation. For a broad learned modification to the existing model, compare full fine-tuning with a parameter-efficient approach.

Third, list operational constraints before training. Include evaluation ownership, permitted data use, artifact storage, deployment compatibility, rollback, monitoring, and the process for replacing or retiring the trained artifact. The risk-management framework's Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage functions provide a first-party structure for organizing these responsibilities [S5].

Fourth, compare candidates on the same held-out cases and acceptance thresholds. Select the least complex intervention that meets the requirement. If no candidate meets it, retain the baseline and revise the data, requirement, or evaluation rather than declaring success.

sections.title: Evaluation and stop rules
paragraphs: Keep training examples separate from the final held-out comparison. Use the held-out set to compare the unchanged baseline, the trained candidate, and any non-training alternative under the same conditions.

Measure what the requirement actually names. A formatting task needs format-validity checks. A classification task needs checks against expected labels and important error types. A retrieval-grounded task needs checks that the retrieved material is relevant and that the answer is supported by it. A compressed student needs comparison with both the teacher and the deployment constraints that motivated compression.

Set stop rules before running the comparison. Stop if the candidate misses a required quality threshold, creates an unacceptable failure, cannot be deployed in the intended environment, or uses data that has not passed the required governance review. These rules prevent a favorable secondary metric from concealing failure on the actual requirement.
sections.callout: A successful training run is not the same as a successful intervention. Success means beating the baseline on the declared acceptance test without violating a stop rule.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes classic adapter training from full fine-tuning?
choices: Classic adapter training keeps the original network parameters fixed and trains added modules, while full fine-tuning updates the original parameters.
Classic adapter training retrieves documents, while full fine-tuning stores documents outside the model.
Classic adapter training trains a separate student, while full fine-tuning never changes model parameters.
Classic adapter training requires no evaluation, while full fine-tuning requires held-out evaluation.
questions.explanation: Classic adapters add trainable modules while keeping the original network parameters fixed. Full fine-tuning updates the original model parameters [S1; S2].

questions.prompt: A team needs answers based on a document collection that changes every week. Which option should it test before trying to encode those facts through training?
choices: Full fine-tuning after every document change
Retrieval that supplies relevant external passages during generation
Distillation without access to the documents
Removing the held-out evaluation
questions.explanation: The module recommends testing retrieval when knowledge changes independently of the model because retrieval supplies external text during generation [S4].

questions.prompt: What is the defining training relationship in knowledge distillation?
choices: A student is trained using a signal that includes a teacher's outputs.
An unchanged model is connected to a document index without training.
All original model parameters are frozen and no other parameters are trained.
A validation set is copied into the training set.
questions.explanation: Knowledge distillation trains a student with a training signal that includes outputs from a teacher, such as softened output distributions [S3].

questions.prompt: When should a team postpone training according to this module?
choices: When it lacks representative evaluation cases and clear expected outcomes
Whenever the base model produces any correct answer
Whenever an adapter approach exists
Whenever the teacher and student are different sizes
questions.explanation: Without representative cases and expected outcomes, the team cannot determine whether training improved the required behavior.

questions.prompt: Which comparison best supports a training decision?
choices: Compare each candidate on a different set of examples.
Compare training loss without testing the unchanged model.
Compare the baseline, trained candidate, and non-training alternative on the same held-out cases.
Select the method that changes the most parameters.
questions.explanation: Using the same held-out cases keeps the acceptance test consistent across the unchanged baseline, the trained candidate, and any non-training alternative.
