modules.title: Mapping our orchestration patterns onto named frameworks
modules.summary: This intermediate module teaches you to compare observable orchestration behavior with ReAct, Plan-and-Solve, and Reflexion without claiming unsupported implementation equivalence. After completing it, you can produce an evidence-based mapping, identify partial matches, and leave an estate-specific classification UNKNOWN when the required evidence is absent.
objectives: Describe the observable characteristics of ReAct, Plan-and-Solve, and Reflexion.
Map an orchestration trace to a named framework using control flow, generated artifacts, feedback, and reuse as evidence.
Distinguish a behavioral resemblance from proof that an implementation uses a particular framework.
Record a partial or UNKNOWN mapping instead of forcing an unsupported classification.
State what additional evidence would resolve an uncertain mapping.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate module. It assumes that you can read a sequence of model requests, external actions, observations, and retries. It does not assume prior knowledge of any named orchestration framework, access to hidden model reasoning, or familiarity with a particular provider.

In this module, orchestration means the observable control flow that coordinates model calls, actions, observations, plans, feedback, and repeated attempts. A mapping compares that observable flow with a documented framework. It does not prove that the implementation imports, copies, or was inspired by the framework.

No trace, design document, or pattern inventory for the estate was supplied with this module. The estate's actual framework mapping is therefore UNKNOWN and is not asserted here. The method below enables a learner to perform that mapping when evidence becomes available.
sections.callout: A responsible mapping names the evidence and its limits. Similar behavior is not proof of implementation identity.

sections.title: Use an evidence-first mapping workflow
paragraphs: Begin with an observable trace or design description. Record the order of events without assigning a framework name. Useful events include creating a plan, selecting an action, receiving an observation, revising a plan, generating feedback after an attempt, and reusing that feedback in a later attempt.

Next, identify the unit being classified. A complete workflow can contain several patterns. For example, one phase might plan before execution while another phase repeatedly alternates actions and observations. Classifying each phase separately prevents a broad workflow label from hiding meaningful differences.

Compare each phase with the defining behavior of a named framework. Record a match only for characteristics visible in the evidence. Also record contradictions and missing evidence. A missing feature is not automatically a contradiction because logging may be incomplete.

Assign a result of match, partial match, no match, or UNKNOWN. Use match when the defining behavior is present, partial match when only some defining behavior is present, no match when evidence contradicts the defining behavior, and UNKNOWN when the available material cannot support a decision.

Finish by stating the scope of the conclusion. A suitable conclusion says that an observed phase is behaviorally consistent with a named framework. It should not say that the estate uses that framework unless implementation records establish that stronger claim.

sections.title: Recognize the ReAct pattern
paragraphs: The ReAct paper presents an approach in which reasoning and actions are interleaved. Actions produce observations, and those observations inform subsequent reasoning and actions. For mapping purposes, the important signature is a repeated cycle rather than a single plan followed by uninterrupted execution.

Evidence consistent with ReAct includes a trace that selects an action, receives an external observation, and then uses that observation before selecting another action. One action alone is insufficient to establish the repeated pattern. A simple request followed by a single response is also insufficient.

Do not require access to hidden model reasoning. If only observable orchestration records are available, classify the visible action and observation loop and state that unobserved reasoning cannot be evaluated. This keeps the conclusion within the available evidence.

sections.title: Recognize the Plan-and-Solve pattern
paragraphs: The Plan-and-Solve paper describes separating planning from solution execution. Its mapping signature is an explicit plan produced before the system carries out the solution steps.

Evidence consistent with Plan-and-Solve includes a plan artifact that decomposes a task and a later execution phase that follows or refers to that plan. Merely performing several steps is not enough because a multistep trace may emerge without a distinct planning phase.

If a system repeatedly replans after every external observation, parts of its behavior may resemble both planning and an interleaved action-observation loop. In that case, classify the phases separately or report a partial match instead of selecting one label for the entire workflow.

sections.title: Recognize the Reflexion pattern
paragraphs: The Reflexion paper describes agents that use linguistic feedback from prior attempts to improve later attempts. Its mapping signature is not merely retrying. The distinguishing evidence is a textual reflection or feedback artifact that is retained and supplied to a subsequent attempt.

Evidence consistent with Reflexion includes an attempt, an evaluation or feedback stage, a generated reflection about what should change, and reuse of that reflection in another attempt. A retry caused only by a transient failure does not establish this pattern.

When a trace shows evaluation but does not show whether feedback is retained or reused, the Reflexion mapping is UNKNOWN or partial, depending on what is visible. Inspecting the inputs to the next attempt would establish whether the reflection was actually reused.

sections.title: Apply the distinctions
paragraphs: Consider a phase that creates a three-step plan and then executes those steps in order. That phase is behaviorally consistent with Plan-and-Solve because planning is separated from execution. If execution later begins alternating actions with observations, that later phase can separately be consistent with ReAct.

Consider a workflow that attempts a task, receives an evaluation, writes a textual account of the failure, and includes that account in the next attempt. That workflow is behaviorally consistent with Reflexion. If the evaluation only triggers the same request again and no reflection is created or reused, the Reflexion label is unsupported.

Consider a log containing repeated external actions but no recorded observations, plans, or feedback artifacts. Several explanations remain possible, including incomplete logging. The correct mapping is UNKNOWN until a fuller trace or design description establishes the missing control flow.

A useful mapping statement has four parts: the phase being classified, the proposed framework, the observed evidence, and the limitation. For example, a planning phase may be described as behaviorally consistent with Plan-and-Solve because a plan precedes execution, while implementation identity remains UNKNOWN because no implementation record is available.

sections.title: Avoid common mapping errors
paragraphs: Do not map by vocabulary alone. A field or log message containing the word plan does not establish a separate planning phase. Inspect when the artifact is created and whether later execution uses it.

Do not treat every action loop as ReAct. Look for observations that affect later action selection. Do not treat every retry as Reflexion. Look for generated feedback that is retained and reused. Do not treat every multistep response as Plan-and-Solve. Look for a distinct plan before execution.

Do not force one label onto a composite workflow. Named patterns can describe different phases, and a phase can only partially resemble a framework. Preserve these distinctions so that the mapping remains useful for design review and comparison.

To complete an estate-specific mapping, obtain representative traces, orchestration design descriptions, and evidence showing which artifacts are passed between attempts. Without those materials, the estate-specific result remains UNKNOWN.

questions.prompt: A trace repeatedly selects an external action, receives an observation, and uses that observation before selecting the next action. Which framework is the strongest behavioral match?
choices: ReAct
Plan-and-Solve
Reflexion
No named pattern can ever be considered
questions.explanation: ReAct is characterized here by an interleaved cycle of reasoning, actions, and observations in which observations inform later steps.

questions.prompt: Which evidence most strongly supports a Plan-and-Solve mapping?
choices: A retry occurs after a transient failure
A plan is created before a separate execution phase that follows it
An external action returns an observation
A framework name appears in a log message
questions.explanation: The distinguishing signature presented in the module is separation between explicit planning and subsequent solution execution.

questions.prompt: A failed attempt is evaluated, a textual reflection is generated, and that reflection is included in the next attempt. Which framework is the strongest behavioral match?
choices: Plan-and-Solve
ReAct
Reflexion
None, because all retries are identical
questions.explanation: Reflexion is distinguished from an ordinary retry by generating linguistic feedback and reusing it in a later attempt.

questions.prompt: A log shows repeated actions but omits observations, plans, and feedback artifacts. What is the most defensible mapping?
choices: ReAct, because every repeated action proves an observation loop
Reflexion, because every repetition proves reflection
Plan-and-Solve, because every multistep process begins with a plan
UNKNOWN until fuller evidence establishes the missing control flow
questions.explanation: The visible log does not establish the defining behavior of any of the three frameworks. Incomplete evidence should produce an UNKNOWN result rather than a forced label.

questions.prompt: What does a behavioral match to a named framework establish?
choices: The implementation must import that framework
The implementation was definitely inspired by the framework's paper
The observed control flow is consistent with the framework within the stated evidence limits
Every phase of the workflow uses the same pattern
questions.explanation: Behavioral mapping compares observable control flow. It does not by itself prove implementation identity, historical influence, or that every phase follows the same pattern.

modules.title: Model Context Protocol and Tool Interoperability
modules.summary: This intermediate module teaches you to reason about Model Context Protocol roles, capability discovery, and interoperable tool use. After completing it, you can trace a tool request across an MCP integration, distinguish protocol compatibility from semantic compatibility, and identify essential validation and authorization controls.
objectives: Explain the responsibilities of an MCP host, client, and server.
Distinguish tools from resources and prompts.
Trace capability discovery and a tool request through an MCP integration.
Assess whether two components are merely protocol-compatible or meaningfully interoperable.
Apply validation, authorization, consent, and least-privilege checks to an MCP tool workflow.

sections.title: Level and learning outcome
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes that you understand basic request and response interactions, structured data, and the difference between reading information and performing an action. It does not assume prior experience implementing Model Context Protocol.

Before this module, you may know that an AI application can connect to external capabilities without being able to explain the roles, negotiation process, or safety boundaries involved. After this module, you will be able to trace an MCP tool request, evaluate whether an integration is genuinely interoperable, and identify where validation and authorization must occur.

sections.title: Why a shared protocol matters
paragraphs: Model Context Protocol, commonly abbreviated MCP, defines a shared way for an AI application to exchange context and capability information with external servers. A shared protocol reduces the need for every application and server pairing to invent a separate interaction format.

Protocol compatibility is only the first layer of interoperability. Two components can exchange valid protocol messages while still disagreeing about the meaning of a field, the units expected by an operation, or the consequences of an action. Meaningful interoperability therefore requires both protocol conformance and clear capability descriptions.

MCP does not make every connected server interchangeable. Servers can expose different capabilities, use different input shapes, and produce different results. An application must inspect what a particular server advertises instead of assuming that every connection offers the same operations.
sections.callout: A shared message format enables communication, but clear semantics and safe behavior make the communication useful.

sections.title: Host, client, and server roles
paragraphs: The host is the application that manages the overall user experience and integration. It decides when external context or actions are appropriate, manages user-facing approval, and applies application security policy.

An MCP client is the host-side protocol participant that maintains a connection with one MCP server. A host can manage multiple clients when it needs to communicate with multiple servers. Keeping each client associated with one server gives the host a clear boundary for routing messages and isolating server interactions.

An MCP server advertises capabilities and handles requests related to those capabilities. A server can provide context, reusable interaction patterns, or callable actions. The server defines what it offers, while the host remains responsible for deciding what the application and user are allowed to use.

These roles are logical responsibilities. Understanding them helps locate failures: connection and routing concerns involve the client relationship, capability behavior involves the server, and user authorization or overall policy belongs with the host.

sections.title: Tools, resources, and prompts
paragraphs: A tool represents an operation that can be invoked with structured input. A tool may retrieve information, perform computation, or cause an external action. Because some tools can change external state, discovering a tool is not the same as receiving permission to invoke it.

A resource provides context that can be read by the application. Resources are appropriate for information that the application may inspect or include as context without treating the read itself as a general-purpose action.

A prompt provides a reusable message template or interaction pattern. It helps package an established way of asking for or organizing work, but it does not replace authorization for any tool that the resulting interaction may invoke.
The distinction matters when designing policy. Reading a resource, selecting a prompt, and invoking a state-changing tool can carry different risks even when the same server exposes all three.

sections.title: Discovery and capability negotiation
paragraphs: An MCP interaction begins by establishing the client-server relationship and exchanging initialization information. During this stage, each side communicates the protocol features it supports. Later behavior should be based on the capabilities actually negotiated, not on assumptions about what every implementation supports.

After initialization, the client can discover the capabilities advertised by the server. For tools, discovery gives the host information such as the operation description and the structured input expected by that operation. The host can use this information to decide whether an invocation is appropriate and to construct valid input.

Capability declarations support interoperability by allowing components to adapt to what is available. They are not authorization grants. A server saying that an operation exists does not establish that a particular user, model, or application may run it.
A robust client treats unsupported capabilities as unavailable. It should not send an operation merely because another server supported it in an earlier connection.
sections.callout: Negotiate first, discover second, authorize third, and invoke only after validation.

sections.title: Tracing an interoperable tool request
paragraphs: First, the server advertises a tool and describes its expected input. The client relays that description within the host, where the application can determine whether the tool is relevant to the user's goal.

Second, the host checks policy and authorization. If the action is consequential or exceeds an existing approval, the host should obtain informed user confirmation before allowing the request to proceed.

Third, the host constructs input that matches the advertised structure. It should validate types, required values, ranges, and any application-specific restrictions before sending the request through the client.

Fourth, the server validates the request again and performs only the operation it is authorized to perform. Validation on the host does not remove the server's responsibility to distrust incoming requests.

Fifth, the result returns through the client to the host. The host should treat returned content as untrusted, check whether it has the expected form, and decide how much of it to expose to the model or user.

Finally, the host presents the outcome and any relevant error in a way the user can understand. This trace separates protocol transport from policy decisions and makes it easier to identify where an unsafe or incompatible interaction occurred.

sections.title: Evaluating interoperability
paragraphs: Begin with protocol compatibility. Confirm that both sides can establish the relationship, negotiate supported capabilities, and exchange the required request and result messages.

Next examine structural compatibility. A client must be able to interpret the server's capability descriptions, construct inputs matching the advertised shapes, and process successful and unsuccessful results.

Then examine semantic compatibility. Names and valid structures are insufficient if the parties disagree about meaning. Descriptions should make the operation's purpose, required inputs, possible effects, and returned information clear enough for the host to make a safe decision.

Finally examine operational compatibility. The integration should handle unavailable capabilities, rejected requests, server errors, and connection loss without silently pretending that the requested action succeeded.

An interoperable design therefore combines negotiation, discovery, clear descriptions, validation, explicit error handling, and policy enforcement. Passing only the message-format layer does not establish that the overall workflow is correct.

sections.title: Security boundaries for tool use
paragraphs: Treat server descriptions, resource contents, tool results, and error text as untrusted input. Content received from a server can be inaccurate or malicious even when the protocol exchange itself is valid.

Apply least privilege. Give each server and tool access only to the information and actions required for its purpose. Avoid treating connection to a server as blanket permission to use everything it advertises.

Keep authorization separate from capability discovery. The host should check user identity, application policy, action sensitivity, and current consent before allowing an invocation. The server should independently enforce the permissions relevant to the external system it controls.
Validate in both directions. Validate requested inputs before invocation, and validate returned content before using it as trusted context or presenting it as a confirmed result.

Preserve a clear user boundary for consequential actions. A model proposing a tool call is not equivalent to a user approving its effects. The host should provide enough information for informed confirmation when confirmation is required.
sections.callout: Capability means an operation is available. Authorization means this requester may use it. Consent means the user has agreed to the relevant effect.

questions.prompt: Which component manages the overall user experience and applies application-level authorization policy?
choices: The host
The server
The resource
The prompt
questions.explanation: The host manages the overall integration, user-facing approval, and application security policy.

questions.prompt: What does a tool represent in this module?
choices: A reusable message template only
A readable source of context only
An operation invoked with structured input
A guarantee that an action is authorized
questions.explanation: A tool is an operation that can be invoked with structured input. Advertising a tool does not grant permission to invoke it.

questions.prompt: What should determine whether a client uses an optional protocol feature?
choices: Whether another server supported it previously
Whether it was negotiated for the current relationship
Whether its name sounds familiar
Whether the model requests it
questions.explanation: Behavior should follow the capabilities negotiated for the current client-server relationship rather than assumptions based on other connections.

questions.prompt: Two components exchange structurally valid messages but disagree about the units expected by a tool input. Which interoperability layer is missing?
choices: Semantic compatibility
Connection routing
User interface styling
Capability discovery
questions.explanation: The message structure is valid, but the parties disagree about meaning. That is a semantic compatibility failure.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes capability from authorization?
choices: If a server advertises a tool, every connected user may invoke it.
Authorization is established automatically during capability discovery.
Capability says an operation is available, while authorization decides whether a requester may use it.
Capability and authorization are two names for the same decision.
questions.explanation: Discovery establishes availability, not permission. The host and server must apply the relevant authorization policies separately.

modules.title: Microsoft Foundry, from provisioning to model deployment
modules.summary: This intermediate-level module teaches you to plan and provision a Microsoft Foundry project, select a suitable model, create a deployment, validate its behavior, and prepare it for application use. After completing it, you can follow a controlled path from an approved cloud scope to a tested model endpoint.
objectives: Explain the roles of a Foundry resource, a project, a model, and a deployment.
Perform a preflight review of access, region, capacity, governance, and model requirements before provisioning.
Provision a project within an approved organizational and billing scope.
Evaluate an available model against task, licensing, interface, and capacity requirements.
Create and validate a model deployment without exposing its credentials.
Record the information an application team needs to consume, monitor, replace, or retire a deployment.

sections.title: Level and assumed knowledge
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes that you understand basic cloud concepts such as regions, access permissions, billing scopes, resource containers, network requests, and model inference. It does not assume that you have previously provisioned Microsoft Foundry or deployed a model there.

The outcome is practical. Before this module, you might recognize Foundry as a place to work with models. After it, you can plan the required boundaries, provision a project, select an appropriate model, deploy it, validate the resulting endpoint, and prepare an operational handoff.

sections.title: Understand the resource chain
paragraphs: Keep four concepts separate. A Foundry resource supplies the cloud context and governance boundary used by Foundry. A project is the workspace in which a team organizes its model work. A model is the selected inference capability. A deployment is a configured, callable instance of that model.

Provisioning and deployment are therefore different operations. Provisioning establishes the resource and project in an approved location and administrative scope. Deployment selects a model and makes it available for inference under a deployment-specific endpoint or connection.

This distinction helps with troubleshooting. If a project cannot be created, investigate scope, region, permissions, and policy. If the project exists but a model cannot be deployed, investigate model availability, capacity, deployment eligibility, and the selected region.
sections.callout: Do not treat project creation as proof that every model can be deployed there. Model availability and capacity must be checked separately.

sections.title: Perform a provisioning preflight
paragraphs: Start with the intended workload rather than the interface. Record the task the model must perform, the expected input and output forms, who may use it, the sensitivity of its data, and how success will be tested. These requirements provide a basis for choosing a model and rejecting unsuitable options.

Confirm the approved billing scope, resource container, region, and access permissions before creating anything. Also identify the person or team authorized to approve cost, model terms, data handling, and production use. If any of those decisions is unresolved, pause rather than creating an unowned resource.

Check that the intended model is offered for the selected region and deployment context. Review the model information presented by Foundry, including intended uses, limitations, applicable terms, supported interfaces, and any capacity requirement. Availability in a model list does not by itself establish suitability for the workload.

Define a simple acceptance test before deployment. Include representative inputs, expected output characteristics, prohibited behavior, and a failure condition. A deployment is technically reachable when it accepts a request, but it is acceptable for use only when it also meets the workload's stated criteria.

sections.title: Provision the Foundry project
paragraphs: Use the documented project-creation flow to select or create the Foundry resource that will back the project, then create the project within the approved scope. Choose only the region and organizational placement approved during the preflight. Use locally defined naming and tagging conventions if your organization has them.

After creation, verify the project boundary before adding a deployment. Confirm that you are in the intended project, that its backing resource and region match the approved plan, and that the expected collaborators have only the access required for their roles.

Record the project owner, purpose, region, billing owner, intended data classification, and review date in the team's operational record. This record is separate from the technical resource. It allows another person to determine why the project exists and who can authorize changes or retirement.

Do not continue if the project appears in an unexpected scope or region. Creating a model deployment in the wrong project compounds the error and can expose the workload to an unapproved policy, access, or cost boundary.

sections.title: Select a model for the workload
paragraphs: Inspect the models available to the project and compare them with the written workload requirements. Begin with task fit and supported input and output forms. Then review limitations, applicable terms, regional availability, capacity, and the deployment choices Foundry presents for that model.

Prefer an explicit decision record over a vague statement that one model seemed best. Record the chosen model, the alternatives considered, the acceptance criteria, known limitations, and the reason for selection. This makes a later model replacement reviewable.

Do not infer that two models are interchangeable because they accept similar prompts. Their output behavior, limitations, terms, capacity needs, and interfaces can differ. Test the exact model and deployment that the application will call.

sections.title: Create the model deployment
paragraphs: Open the selected model's deployment flow and choose only an option that Foundry makes available for the current project and region. Review the displayed model, region, capacity implications, and applicable terms before confirming. If required capacity is unavailable, return to planning rather than silently changing the workload requirement.

Give the deployment an identity that follows the organization's naming convention and distinguishes its purpose or environment. Avoid placing secrets, personal data, or sensitive business information in the deployment identity or descriptive metadata.

Submit the deployment and wait for its reported state to indicate that it is ready before testing it. A submitted operation is not the same as a usable deployment. If creation fails, preserve the reported error and recheck permissions, availability, capacity, region, and policy rather than repeatedly submitting the same request.

Once ready, identify the connection information the approved application needs. Treat credentials as secrets. Do not paste them into source code, shared documents, test prompts, or operational notes. Provide them through the organization's approved secret-handling process.

sections.title: Validate and hand off the deployment
paragraphs: First perform a connectivity check with a non-sensitive input. Confirm that the request reaches the intended deployment and produces a response. This proves basic reachability, not model quality or production readiness.

Next run the acceptance test defined during the preflight. Use representative inputs and compare the outputs with the recorded criteria. Test relevant failure cases, such as malformed or unsupported input, without using confidential data unless the workload and its data handling have been approved for that purpose.

Record the tested deployment identity, model, project, region, test date, acceptance result, known limitations, owner, and retirement or review trigger. Give the application team only the endpoint details and access path it needs. Do not include secret values in the handoff record.

Prepare a replacement and recovery plan before production use. Keep the previous acceptable deployment available when organizational policy and cost constraints permit, verify a replacement before directing application traffic to it, and define who can approve the switch. If validation fails, do not promote the new deployment.

After traffic moves or an experiment ends, review unused deployments and resources for retirement. Confirm dependencies and retention obligations before deletion. Record the decision so that an apparently unused deployment is not removed without an accountable review.
sections.callout: A successful response proves connectivity. Production readiness also requires documented quality, security, governance, ownership, and recovery checks.

sections.title: Apply the end-to-end sequence
paragraphs: The complete sequence is to define the workload, confirm governance and regional constraints, define acceptance tests, provision the correct resource and project, verify their boundaries, evaluate available models, create the selected deployment, wait for readiness, test connectivity, run acceptance tests, secure connection information, document ownership, and prepare replacement and retirement procedures.

Each stage has a distinct completion condition. Provisioning is complete when the intended project exists in the approved boundary and ownership is recorded. Deployment is complete when the selected model has a ready deployment. Validation is complete only when the exact deployment passes the predetermined tests. Handoff is complete when an application team can connect through an approved access path and operators know how to review, replace, or retire the deployment.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes provisioning from model deployment?
choices: Provisioning establishes the resource and project boundary, while deployment creates a callable instance of a selected model.
Provisioning tests model output quality, while deployment assigns project permissions.
Provisioning and deployment are two names for the same operation.
Provisioning begins only after an application has entered production.
questions.explanation: The module defines provisioning as establishing the Foundry resource and project context. Deployment selects and configures a model so that it can be called for inference.

questions.prompt: What should happen before resources are created?
choices: The team should select whichever model appears first.
The team should confirm workload requirements, scope, region, permissions, governance ownership, and acceptance criteria.
The team should distribute credentials to all collaborators.
The team should assume that every listed model is available in every project.
questions.explanation: The preflight establishes the workload, approved boundary, access, ownership, model constraints, and tests before provisioning begins.

questions.prompt: A new deployment returns a response to a test request. What has this established?
choices: The deployment is ready for every production workload.
The model has no limitations.
Basic connectivity works, but quality and production-readiness checks are still required.
The deployment can safely process every data classification.
questions.explanation: A successful request proves basic reachability. The module requires separate acceptance, governance, security, ownership, and recovery checks.

questions.prompt: How should deployment credentials be handled during handoff?
choices: Place them directly in application source code.
Include them in the shared operational record.
Send them as part of a test prompt.
Provide them through the organization's approved secret-handling process.
questions.explanation: The module says to treat credentials as secrets and to keep secret values out of source code, shared documents, prompts, and operational notes.

questions.prompt: What is the correct response when a replacement deployment fails its acceptance test?
choices: Promote it because it is technically reachable.
Do not promote it, preserve the evidence, and investigate the failed criteria.
Delete every previous deployment immediately.
Change the acceptance criteria after seeing the output.
questions.explanation: The module states that a new deployment must pass predetermined acceptance tests before promotion. A failure should be investigated rather than hidden by changing the criteria.

modules.title: Agent orchestration and multi-agent patterns
modules.summary: This intermediate module teaches you to design, trace, and evaluate workflows in which multiple agents coordinate through explicit roles, messages, state, and stopping rules. After completing it, you can choose an orchestration pattern for a task and specify the controls needed to operate it safely.
objectives: Distinguish an agent from the orchestration logic that coordinates agents.
Map a task to sequential, parallel, supervisor-worker, shared-workspace, or debate-and-critique patterns.
Define agent roles, message contracts, state ownership, completion conditions, and failure handling.
Trace a multi-agent run and identify duplicated work, unsafe actions, missing evidence, and unresolved disagreement.
Design bounded workflows with explicit permissions, budgets, validation steps, and escalation paths.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate module. It assumes that you understand basic model requests and responses, structured data, conditional control flow, and the difference between instructions and generated output. No previous multi-agent experience is assumed.

An agent is a bounded participant that receives context, performs reasoning or actions allowed by its role, and returns a result. Orchestration is the control logic that decides which agent acts, what context it receives, where its output goes, and when the workflow stops. A multi-agent system uses more than one such participant, but adding participants does not automatically improve a result.

The practical goal is not to imitate a human organization. It is to divide work only when the division creates a useful boundary, such as a distinct capability, independent review, restricted permission, or parallel task.
sections.callout: Treat orchestration as a controlled workflow, not as an unrestricted conversation.

sections.title: Core design elements
paragraphs: A role definition states an agent's responsibility, permitted inputs, permitted actions, expected output, and conditions for returning control. Narrow roles make routing and evaluation easier. Labels such as researcher or reviewer are insufficient unless their permissions and output obligations are also defined.

A message contract specifies the structure and meaning of information exchanged between participants. It should distinguish claims, evidence, unresolved questions, requested actions, and status. Validate a message before another participant or an external system relies on it. Generated text remains untrusted input even when it comes from another agent.

State records what the workflow currently knows and what has happened. Private state belongs to one participant. Shared state is visible to several participants. Durable run state supports recovery and auditing. State ownership must be explicit so that concurrent participants do not silently overwrite one another.

A stopping rule defines success, failure, or escalation. Useful signals include acceptance by a validator, completion of all required tasks, exhaustion of a declared budget, detection of repeated states, or a request for human review. A request to continue is not itself evidence that continued work will help.

sections.title: The orchestration loop
paragraphs: A controlled run begins by converting the user's request into a task record with a goal, constraints, required evidence, allowed actions, and completion criteria. The orchestrator then selects an eligible participant, supplies only the necessary context, validates the response, updates state, and chooses the next transition.

Separate generation from control. A participant may propose a next action, but the orchestrator should determine whether that action is permitted and whether its arguments satisfy the required contract. This separation limits the effect of an erroneous or manipulated proposal.

Record each transition with the acting participant, input reference, output reference, validation result, action result, and reason for the next routing decision. A trace should make it possible to reconstruct why the workflow reached its final state without relying on hidden conversational context.

Before returning a result, apply a final acceptance check against the original goal and constraints. Completion means that the stated criteria have been met, not merely that no participant has another suggestion.

sections.title: Sequential handoff
paragraphs: In a sequential handoff, one participant's validated output becomes the next participant's input. This pattern fits work with a real dependency order, such as producing a draft before reviewing it and revising only after review.

The main design risk is error propagation. Later participants may treat an earlier claim as established simply because it appears in the shared context. Preserve evidence references and uncertainty markers at every handoff, and require downstream participants to reject inputs that fail their contracts.
Use sequential handoff when each stage transforms or checks the result of the preceding stage. Do not use it merely to make several participants restate the same task.

sections.title: Parallel fan-out and fan-in
paragraphs: In parallel fan-out, the orchestrator sends independent subtasks or alternative approaches to multiple participants. A fan-in stage then validates and combines their results. This pattern can reduce elapsed time when subtasks are genuinely independent, although it increases coordination work and does not guarantee a better answer.

The fan-in rule must be defined before execution. It may require all mandatory subtasks, select a result that passes a validator, merge non-overlapping fields, or escalate incompatible findings. A simple majority is not an evidence check because several participants can repeat the same unsupported claim.

Parallel work is unsuitable when participants must repeatedly edit the same state or when one task depends on an unfinished result from another. In those cases, explicit dependencies or sequential transitions are safer.

sections.title: Supervisor-worker delegation
paragraphs: In a supervisor-worker pattern, a coordinating participant decomposes a goal and proposes assignments to specialized workers. The orchestrator still enforces permissions, validates assignments, and applies stopping rules. The supervisor is a planner within the workflow, not an authority outside its controls.

Each assignment should contain a bounded objective, relevant context, allowed actions, expected output, and a return condition. The supervisor should receive summaries and evidence references rather than every intermediate token unless full detail is required.

This pattern is useful when decomposition depends on information discovered during the run. Its risks include unnecessary delegation, recursive task creation, duplicated assignments, and a supervisor accepting plausible but unsupported reports. Limit delegation depth, track task identities, and validate worker outputs before closing tasks.

sections.title: Shared workspace
paragraphs: In a shared-workspace pattern, participants contribute records to a common state and read contributions made by others. This can support tasks where partial findings need to accumulate without a fixed handoff order.

Shared state needs a schema, ownership rules, provenance, and conflict handling. Append-only observations are easier to audit than silent replacement. If an item can change, store its author, status, evidence, and revision history so that disagreement remains visible.
Do not place secrets or unrestricted action authority in shared state merely for convenience. Give each participant the least context and permission needed for its assignment.

sections.title: Debate and critique
paragraphs: A debate-and-critique pattern asks participants to produce competing proposals, inspect one another's reasoning, or challenge specific claims. Research has investigated multi-agent debate as a way to improve reasoning and factuality in selected evaluations, but that does not establish that debate improves every task.

A useful critique identifies a claim, explains the defect, and requests evidence or a correction. Repeated disagreement without a decision rule creates cost without resolution. The workflow therefore needs an adjudication rule, such as evidence validation, an independent rubric, or human escalation.

Keep diversity of evidence separate from the number of voices. Several outputs derived from the same context can share the same error. The final decision should depend on validated support and task criteria rather than confidence, verbosity, or voting alone.

sections.title: Choosing a pattern
paragraphs: Start with the simplest workflow that meets the task's needs. Choose sequential handoff for true dependencies, parallel fan-out for independent work, supervisor-worker delegation for adaptive decomposition, a shared workspace for accumulating contributions, and debate or critique for structured challenge.

Patterns can be composed. For example, a supervisor may create independent assignments, workers may run in parallel, and a validator may inspect the combined result. Each composition adds transitions and failure modes, so every added participant should have a stated purpose.

Ask five questions before adding an agent: What distinct responsibility does it have? What information may it receive? What actions may it take? How is its output validated? What condition returns control? If these questions have no clear answers, a separate agent boundary is probably not yet justified.

sections.title: Reliability and safety controls
paragraphs: Bound the workflow with limits on work, time, delegated tasks, retries, and allowed actions. The specific limits depend on the application and must be chosen from operational requirements rather than copied from an unrelated system.

Use idempotent action handling where practical so that retrying a recorded request does not unintentionally repeat an external effect. Before a consequential action, check authorization, validate arguments, detect whether the action already succeeded, and record the outcome.

Treat content from users, external data, and other participants as untrusted. Instructions found inside retrieved content should not silently replace the workflow's governing rules. Restrict context and action permissions at each boundary.

Define failure handling for malformed messages, unavailable capabilities, timeouts, contradictory state, failed actions, and exhausted budgets. Recovery may retry a safe operation, choose another path, restore a checkpoint, return a partial result with limitations, or escalate to a person.

Human review is most valuable at explicit decision points, especially when evidence is insufficient, policy interpretation is required, effects are difficult to reverse, or participants remain in material disagreement.

sections.title: Evaluation and debugging
paragraphs: Evaluate both the final result and the process. Result measures can cover correctness, evidence quality, completeness, and adherence to constraints. Process measures can cover unnecessary transitions, duplicated tasks, invalid messages, failed actions, unresolved conflicts, and escalation behavior.

Test individual roles with fixed inputs before testing the full workflow. Then test transitions, shared-state updates, permission checks, stopping rules, retries, and recovery paths. Include adversarial cases in which a participant proposes a prohibited action, supplies malformed output, repeats an earlier state, or asserts completion without meeting the acceptance criteria.

When a run fails, inspect the first transition where state diverged from the intended contract. A poor final answer may originate in task decomposition, omitted context, invalid routing, weak validation, an unsafe action, or an incorrect stopping decision. Changing a participant's instructions will not repair every class of orchestration failure.

sections.title: Design walkthrough
paragraphs: Consider a task that requires collecting independent findings, drafting a response, and checking every factual claim. A suitable design can fan out bounded research assignments, store findings with evidence references, pass only validated findings to a drafting participant, and send the draft to a reviewer.

The reviewer returns structured findings rather than silently rewriting the draft. Each finding identifies the affected claim, the evidence issue, and the requested correction. The orchestrator routes accepted corrections back to the drafting stage and stops only when the acceptance check passes or a declared limit requires escalation.

This design gives every participant a distinct responsibility. It also preserves evidence through handoffs, prevents the reviewer from bypassing validation, and creates a trace of why the final response was accepted. After this module, you can produce the same kind of pattern selection, role contract, transition plan, and control checklist for your own task.

questions.prompt: Which responsibility belongs to orchestration rather than to an individual agent role?
choices: Deciding which eligible participant acts next and when the workflow stops
Writing the content assigned to a drafting role
Finding evidence assigned to a research role
Explaining a defect assigned to a critique role
questions.explanation: Orchestration controls routing, state transitions, validation, and stopping. The other choices are responsibilities that can be assigned to bounded participant roles.

questions.prompt: A task contains several independent subtasks whose results must all be validated and combined. Which pattern is the best initial match?
choices: An unrestricted conversation
Parallel fan-out followed by fan-in
A sequential handoff with no validation
Repeated debate with no adjudication rule
questions.explanation: Parallel fan-out fits genuinely independent work, and fan-in supplies the required validation and combination step.

questions.prompt: Why is a majority vote among agents not sufficient evidence that a claim is correct?
choices: Agents are unable to return structured messages
Agents cannot work in parallel
Several participants can repeat the same unsupported claim
Voting always violates a stopping rule
questions.explanation: Multiple outputs may share the same unsupported assumption or source. Claims should be judged through validated evidence and task criteria, not vote count alone.

questions.prompt: Which assignment is best bounded for a worker?
choices: Help with the project however you think best
Keep creating tasks until nothing else can be imagined
Complete the entire goal and use any action you want
Investigate the specified subquestion using the supplied context, return claims with evidence references, and take no external action
questions.explanation: The correct assignment has a specific objective, bounded context, an expected output, and explicit action limits.

questions.prompt: What should completion mean in a controlled multi-agent workflow?
choices: The workflow's stated acceptance criteria have been met
The last participant produced a confident answer
Every participant agrees, regardless of evidence
No participant has requested another message
questions.explanation: The module defines completion against the original goal and constraints. Confidence, agreement, or conversational silence does not establish success.

modules.title: Retrieval-augmented generation, embeddings, and vector search
modules.summary: This intermediate module teaches you to design and evaluate a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline. After completing it, you can explain how embeddings and vector search connect a question to relevant source text, choose between exact and approximate search, and diagnose retrieval separately from answer generation.
objectives: Describe the indexing, retrieval, and generation stages of a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline.
Explain how compatible document and query embeddings make semantic vector search possible.
Compare dot-product, cosine-similarity, and Euclidean-distance scoring at a conceptual level.
Choose between exact and approximate nearest-neighbor search based on measured retrieval quality and resource constraints.
Evaluate retrieval and answer generation separately so that failures can be traced to the correct stage.

sections.title: Level and learning outcome
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It defines its retrieval terminology and assumes only a basic understanding that a language model accepts text as input and produces text as output. It does not assume experience with a particular product, hosted service, vector index, or embedding implementation.

Before this module, you may know that external documents can help a language model answer questions. After it, you will be able to map that idea into an indexing, retrieval, and generation pipeline; reason about similarity scoring; and test whether a weak answer was caused by retrieval or by generation.

sections.title: The retrieval-augmented generation mental model
paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation, commonly shortened to RAG, combines a generator with a retrievable collection of external text. The Retrieval-Augmented Generation paper describes this as combining parametric memory in a language model with non-parametric memory represented by a dense vector index. In practical terms, the system searches an external collection at question time and supplies selected text to the generator.

A basic RAG pipeline has two paths. The offline indexing path prepares source documents, divides them into retrievable passages, computes vector representations, and records the relationship between each vector and its source text. The online path embeds a user's question, searches for nearby passage vectors, obtains the corresponding text, and gives the question plus that text to the generator.

The retrieved text is context, not proof that the final answer is correct. Retrieval can return an irrelevant passage, omit a necessary passage, or return outdated material. A generator can also produce a statement that the retrieved text does not support. RAG therefore creates a way to use external evidence, but it does not guarantee a supported answer.
sections.callout: Keep the stages separate: indexing prepares searchable material, retrieval selects material for a question, and generation produces the response.

sections.title: Embeddings and compatible vector spaces
paragraphs: An embedding is a fixed-length numeric vector used to represent an input such as a passage or a question. Dense retrieval compares these vectors rather than requiring an exact match between every word in the question and every word in a passage. The Dense Passage Retrieval paper demonstrates retrieval with dense passage and question representations.

The query and document representations must be compatible for their similarity scores to be meaningful. They may be produced by one shared mapping or by separate query and passage mappings trained to place related inputs in a compatible vector space. A vector from an unrelated embedding space must not be compared as though it belonged to the indexed space.

An indexed record needs more than a vector. It also needs a stable link back to the passage and its source information. Without that link, the search stage can identify a nearby vector but cannot recover the text that the generator needs.

Passage boundaries are a design decision rather than a universal constant. A passage must contain enough context to be useful while remaining focused enough for retrieval. The appropriate boundary and amount of overlap should be selected through evaluation on representative questions rather than assumed in advance.

sections.title: Vector search and similarity scoring
paragraphs: Vector search ranks indexed vectors in relation to a query vector. With dot-product scoring, a larger dot product indicates a higher ranking. Cosine similarity divides the dot product by the product of the vectors' lengths, so it compares direction rather than raw magnitude. Euclidean distance measures straight-line distance, and a smaller distance indicates a nearer vector.

If every compared vector has unit length, ranking by cosine similarity is the same as ranking by dot product. For unit-length vectors, squared Euclidean distance also produces the reverse ordering because the squared distance equals two minus twice the dot product. These relationships do not justify switching scoring rules when vectors are not normalized or when the embedding procedure expects a particular rule.

Exact nearest-neighbor search evaluates the indexed candidates needed to identify the true nearest results under the selected score. Approximate nearest-neighbor search uses an index structure to avoid evaluating every candidate, accepting that it may miss a true nearest result. The Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs paper presents one graph-based method for approximate nearest-neighbor search.

The choice between exact and approximate search is an engineering decision that should be measured. Relevant observations include retrieval quality on labeled questions, response time, memory use, and collection size. Approximate search is not automatically the correct choice, and its effect on relevant-passage retrieval should be tested.

sections.title: Building a traceable pipeline
paragraphs: Start by defining the source collection and the questions it is intended to answer. Preserve enough source information to identify where every passage came from. Then divide the source text into passages, compute compatible passage embeddings, and store each vector with a reference to its passage.

At question time, compute a compatible query embedding and search the passage vectors using the scoring rule expected by the embedding procedure. Select a limited set of highly ranked passages and recover their text. Give the generator the question, the retrieved text, and a clear instruction to distinguish supported information from missing information.

Keep a trace for evaluation. At minimum, the trace should connect the question to its query representation, ranked passage identifiers, similarity scores, recovered source text, and generated answer. This trace makes it possible to inspect the boundary between retrieval and generation without assuming that the final answer alone reveals the cause of a failure.

When the collection changes, the searchable records must continue to correspond to the intended source text. A pipeline should therefore define how changed or removed passages are reflected in the index. The appropriate update process depends on the collection and should be validated rather than inferred from a successful initial build.

sections.title: Evaluating retrieval and generation separately
paragraphs: A useful evaluation set pairs representative questions with passages judged relevant to those questions and with criteria for an acceptable answer. Retrieval can then be measured before the generator is involved. For example, recall at k is the fraction of evaluated questions for which at least one judged-relevant passage appears among the first k retrieved passages.

Generation should be evaluated with the retrieved text visible. Check whether the answer addresses the question, whether its factual statements are supported by that text, and whether it clearly indicates when the provided material is insufficient. This separates answer behavior from the earlier question of whether the necessary evidence was retrieved.

Diagnosis follows the stage boundaries. If a relevant passage exists in the collection but does not appear in the retrieved set, investigate passage boundaries, query and passage compatibility, scoring, and search behavior. If the relevant passage is retrieved but the answer contradicts or ignores it, investigate the generation instructions and answer evaluation. If the needed information is absent from the collection, changing similarity search alone cannot supply that missing information.

Compare pipeline changes on the same evaluation set. A change that improves retrieval recall but reduces answer support is not an unqualified improvement. The goal is a measured end-to-end system in which retrieval supplies useful evidence and generation uses that evidence appropriately.
sections.callout: Do not use answer quality as the only retrieval metric. Inspect whether the required passage was retrieved before judging how the generator used it.

questions.prompt: Which sequence correctly describes the online path of the basic pipeline taught in this module?
choices: Generate an answer, embed the answer, and then divide the sources into passages
Embed the question, search passage vectors, recover passage text, and generate an answer using that text
Remove passage identifiers, compare source filenames, and generate an embedding
Generate new source documents and then search the generated answer
questions.explanation: The online path embeds the question, searches the indexed passage vectors, recovers the associated text, and supplies that text with the question to the generator.

questions.prompt: Under which condition does this module say cosine similarity gives the same ranking as dot-product scoring?
choices: Every compared vector has unit length
Every passage contains the same number of words
The collection contains only one document
The generator has already produced an answer
questions.explanation: For unit-length vectors, cosine similarity equals the dot product, so both produce the same ranking.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes approximate nearest-neighbor search from exact nearest-neighbor search in this module?
choices: Approximate search guarantees that every returned passage is factually correct
Approximate search avoids evaluating every candidate but may miss a true nearest result
Approximate search does not use vectors
Approximate search generates passages instead of retrieving them
questions.explanation: Approximate search reduces candidate evaluation through an index structure, with the stated possibility that a true nearest result may be missed.

questions.prompt: A relevant passage is among the top retrieved results, but the answer contradicts that passage. Which stage should be investigated first?
choices: Generation instructions and answer evaluation
Whether the source collection contains the passage
Whether the passage has a stable identifier
Whether exact search evaluated enough indexed candidates
questions.explanation: Because the relevant passage was successfully retrieved, the first investigation should focus on how generation used or ignored that context.

questions.prompt: What does recall at k measure in the evaluation approach described here?
choices: The fraction of evaluated questions with at least one judged-relevant passage in the first k results
The number of words generated after retrieving k passages
The fraction of indexed vectors that have unit length
The time required to divide one document into k passages
questions.explanation: The module defines recall at k as the fraction of evaluated questions for which at least one judged-relevant passage appears among the first k retrieved passages.

modules.title: Embeddings and vector stores
modules.summary: This intermediate module teaches you to design an embedding-based retrieval workflow, choose between exact and approximate search, and evaluate whether retrieved records are useful. After completing it, you can describe and troubleshoot the path from source content to vectors, stored records, similarity search, and retrieved context.
objectives: Explain how an embedding represents an input as a numeric vector for similarity comparison.
Design a vector-store record that connects an embedding to its source content and provenance.
Trace a query through embedding, similarity search, filtering, and content retrieval.
Choose between exact and approximate nearest-neighbor search for a stated retrieval requirement.
Evaluate retrieval with labeled queries and diagnose failures involving segmentation, representation, search, or source content.

sections.title: Level and learning outcomes
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes that you understand arrays, records, basic functions, and the difference between stored data and a query. It introduces the vector-search concepts it uses and does not assume prior knowledge of machine-learning training or advanced linear algebra.

Before this module, you may know that semantic retrieval uses embeddings without being able to design or test the complete workflow. Afterward, you can map source content into retrievable records, explain how similarity search selects candidates, decide whether exact or approximate search fits a requirement, and evaluate retrieval failures systematically.

sections.title: What an embedding represents
paragraphs: An embedding procedure maps an input, such as text, to a fixed-length numeric vector. Research on distributed representations demonstrates that learned vectors can encode relationships that support similarity comparisons. Sources: Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality, https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.4546, checked 2026-08-20; Billion-scale similarity search with GPUs, https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.08734, checked 2026-08-20.

The vector is useful because a retrieval system can compare it with other vectors. Individual coordinates should not be treated as independently authored labels. The useful information is distributed across the representation and interpreted through comparisons in its vector space. Source: Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality, https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.4546, checked 2026-08-20.

A query vector and stored vectors must be created by compatible embedding procedures that place them in a shared comparison space. Retrieval-augmented generation research demonstrates this pattern with a query encoder and a dense vector index of documents. Source: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks, https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401, checked 2026-08-20.

Treat the embedding procedure and the source record as separate parts of the design. The procedure creates a representation for comparison, while the source record supplies the content, identifier, and provenance that an application needs after retrieval.
sections.callout: An embedding is a representation used for comparison. It is not the original content, a citation, or proof that the content is correct.

sections.title: What the vector store must retain
paragraphs: In this module, a vector store means a data system that retains vectors and enough associated information to find the corresponding source records. A practical record design contains a stable record identifier, the vector, the retrievable content or a resolvable content locator, and provenance such as a source identifier.

The vector supports candidate selection, but the identifier or locator reconnects a candidate to usable content. Dense retrieval research follows this separation by searching a vector index and then using the retrieved documents as non-parametric memory. Source: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks, https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401, checked 2026-08-20.

Metadata can be retained for application rules such as access scope, document type, language, or publication state. Decide which fields are required before indexing, because a vector alone does not contain the source record or its operational provenance.

When source content changes, use a defined update process for both the source record and its vector. This is a design rule: the stored representation and the content returned for that record should refer to the same indexed state.

sections.title: Preparing content for indexing
paragraphs: Long source material is commonly divided into retrieval units before embedding. Retrieval-augmented generation research demonstrates retrieval over document passages held in a dense vector index. Source: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks, https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401, checked 2026-08-20.

Segmentation defines what one search result can return. A very broad unit may mix several subjects, while a narrow unit may omit context needed to interpret the passage. These are possible failure modes to test rather than universal size rules.

For each unit, preserve a stable link to its parent source and enough location information to recover context. Then create its embedding and store the vector with the record identifier and provenance. Do not claim one universally correct unit size. Select segmentation rules with representative queries and evaluate the resulting retrieval.

sections.title: Similarity and nearest-neighbor search
paragraphs: Similarity search receives a query vector and looks for stored vectors that are closest according to a chosen comparison rule. Published similarity-search research describes nearest-neighbor retrieval over large vector collections and evaluates both Euclidean-distance and inner-product search settings. Source: Billion-scale similarity search with GPUs, https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.08734, checked 2026-08-20.

The comparison rule is part of the retrieval design because it determines what closest means. Use the rule intended for the embedding procedure, and keep that rule consistent while comparing evaluation results.

Exact search examines the collection sufficiently to identify the true nearest results under the selected rule. Approximate nearest-neighbor methods trade a guarantee of exact results for more efficient search over large collections. Research on hierarchical navigable small-world graphs evaluates this trade-off using search performance and recall. Source: Efficient and robust approximate nearest neighbor search using Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs, https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09320, checked 2026-08-20.

Choose exact search when exact nearest results are required and the workload permits it. Consider approximate search when measured retrieval quality remains acceptable and search efficiency is a binding requirement. This decision must be based on measurements from the intended collection and queries rather than on an assumed universal threshold.

sections.title: Tracing a retrieval request
paragraphs: A retrieval request can be traced through five conceptual stages. First, validate the query and any application constraints. Second, create a query embedding with a procedure compatible with the indexed vectors. Third, search for nearby vectors under the selected comparison rule. Fourth, apply required record-selection rules at a defined point in the workflow. Fifth, resolve the selected identifiers to source content and return the content with provenance.

Dense retrieval research supports the central sequence of encoding a query, searching a dense vector index, and retrieving documents for downstream use. Source: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks, https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401, checked 2026-08-20.

Record-selection rules and vector similarity answer different questions. Similarity ranks candidates under the vector comparison, while a selection rule decides whether a record is eligible for the request. Document whether eligibility is enforced before or after candidate generation so that missing results can be diagnosed.
Keep the retrieved identifier, source location, and similarity output available during testing. They let you distinguish a poor candidate ranking from a failure to resolve the correct source record.

sections.title: Evaluating retrieval quality
paragraphs: Build a test set of representative queries with judgments identifying acceptable source records. For a selected result count, mark a query successful when at least one acceptable record appears in the returned set. Report the number of successful queries divided by the number of evaluated queries, and retain the individual failures for inspection.

Approximate nearest-neighbor research uses recall to measure how well approximate results reproduce desired neighbors, demonstrating that retrieval quality and search performance should be measured together. Source: Efficient and robust approximate nearest neighbor search using Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs, https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09320, checked 2026-08-20.

Diagnose a failed query in stages. Check whether the needed content exists in the indexed sources, whether segmentation produced a useful retrieval unit, whether the compatible embedding procedure was used, whether record-selection rules excluded the target, whether approximate search missed a desired neighbor, and whether the chosen result count was sufficient.

A nearby vector is not automatically a correct answer. It is a candidate selected under the embedding representation and comparison rule. Downstream use should preserve source provenance and apply any separate checks required by the application.
sections.callout: Evaluate retrieval separately from any downstream answer-generation step. Otherwise, a fluent answer can hide a missing or irrelevant retrieval result.

questions.prompt: Which record design best supports returning usable source content after a similarity search?
choices: Store only the vector because its coordinates contain the complete source record.
Store the vector with a stable record identifier and source content or a resolvable content locator.
Store only the query that was used to create the vector.
Store a similarity score permanently without retaining source provenance.
questions.explanation: The module specifies that the vector selects candidates, while an identifier, content field, or resolvable locator reconnects each candidate to usable source content and provenance.

questions.prompt: Why must query vectors and stored vectors be created by compatible embedding procedures?
choices: So they occupy a shared comparison space in which similarity search is meaningful.
So every source record has identical text.
So record identifiers can be removed.
So approximate search always returns exact results.
questions.explanation: The module states that query and stored vectors need compatible embedding procedures that place them in a shared comparison space.

questions.prompt: When is approximate nearest-neighbor search an appropriate choice according to this module?
choices: Whenever no retrieval evaluation is available.
When exact results are mandatory regardless of workload.
When measured retrieval quality is acceptable and search efficiency is a binding requirement.
When the source content has no stable identifiers.
questions.explanation: The module recommends considering approximate search only when its measured retrieval quality remains acceptable and efficiency is a binding requirement.

questions.prompt: A relevant source exists, but no acceptable record is retrieved. Which diagnostic sequence best follows the module?
choices: Inspect segmentation, embedding compatibility, selection rules, approximate-search behavior, and the selected result count.
Assume that a nearby vector must contain the correct answer.
Remove provenance fields and repeat the same request.
Judge retrieval only by the fluency of a downstream generated answer.
questions.explanation: The module directs the learner to inspect the retrieval pipeline in stages, including segmentation, representation, eligibility rules, search behavior, and result count.
