modules.title: Voice agents, virtual instructors, and accessible media
modules.summary: This intermediate module enables learners to design a provider-neutral conversational learning experience that coordinates voice interaction, instructional dialogue, accessible media alternatives, recovery paths, and human review. After completing it, learners can turn a learning objective into an interaction flow and evaluate whether that flow remains usable when speech recognition, generated responses, or media access fails.
objectives: Map a voice interaction into input, interpretation, dialogue, response, output, and recovery stages.
Design a virtual instructor around a measurable learning objective rather than unrestricted conversation.
Select captions, transcripts, audio descriptions, and non-voice controls for different access needs.
Create confirmation, correction, fallback, and human-escalation paths for consequential interactions.
Plan an evaluation that measures task completion, instructional progress, accessibility, failures, and recovery.
Identify privacy and safety decisions that must be settled before collecting or retaining voice interaction data.

sections.title: Scope and assumed knowledge
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes basic familiarity with conversational interfaces, digital media playback, learning objectives, and user testing. It does not assume programming knowledge, knowledge of a named provider, or experience with a particular implementation.

A voice agent accepts spoken input and can return a spoken or non-spoken response. A virtual instructor is the instructional role played by a conversational system. The two concepts overlap, but they are not identical: a virtual instructor can use text, and a voice agent can perform tasks that have no teaching purpose.

Accessible media provides equivalent or complementary ways to obtain information presented through sound or images. The appropriate alternative depends on what the original medium communicates. Captions represent speech and relevant audio in synchronized text, transcripts provide a text record, and audio descriptions communicate important visual information that the main audio does not convey. Sources 2, 3, and 4 document these distinctions.

After this module, the learner should be able to move from a broad idea such as creating a speaking tutor to a reviewable interaction design with explicit instructional goals, media alternatives, failure recovery, and evaluation criteria.

sections.title: Model the complete voice interaction
paragraphs: Treat voice interaction as a sequence rather than a single act. A useful provider-neutral model contains input capture, recognition of spoken input, interpretation of the request, selection or generation of a response, production of spoken output, and recovery. Dialogue-system literature describes comparable modular and end-to-end approaches, as summarized in Source 1.

At each stage, record the expected input, expected output, uncertainty that can arise, and available recovery action. Background noise may affect captured input, recognition may produce the wrong words, interpretation may assign the wrong intent, and a generated response may be irrelevant or unsupported. The design should not hide these possibilities behind a fluent voice.

A visible or spoken confirmation is appropriate when a mistaken interpretation could materially affect the learner. Confirmation can repeat the interpreted request and offer correction before an action proceeds. For low-consequence turns, repeated confirmation can obstruct the interaction, so the design decision should follow the consequence of an error rather than a universal rule.

Recovery paths can include asking the learner to repeat or rephrase, showing the recognized text for editing, offering a small set of choices, switching to text input, returning to the previous step, or requesting human assistance. A fallback is part of the primary design, not an exception to be added after deployment.

sections.title: Design the virtual instructor as a teaching system
paragraphs: Begin with a measurable learning objective. Then define the evidence that would demonstrate progress, such as a correct explanation, a completed procedure, or an accurate choice with reasoning. Conversation is the delivery mechanism, not the objective.

A bounded instructional turn can present a task, collect the learner's response, check it against known criteria, provide feedback, offer a hint, and decide whether to continue, retry, review prerequisite material, or escalate. This structure makes the instructional decision observable and testable.

Separate feedback from unsupported judgment. When the system has an established answer or rubric, it can compare a response with those criteria and explain the comparison. When it lacks sufficient evidence, it should state that it cannot determine correctness rather than inventing certainty. No claim is made here that conversational delivery automatically improves learning outcomes.

Give learners control over pace and modality. They should be able to pause, repeat, skip where instruction permits, inspect text, correct recognized input, and leave the interaction. For an important assessment or high-consequence decision, define when a person reviews the result instead of allowing the conversational system to be the final authority.

sections.title: Provide access beyond the spoken channel
paragraphs: Voice should not be the only route to information or control. Provide a text path for entering requests and reading responses when the interaction permits it. Controls needed to operate the experience should also be available without requiring speech.

Captions are synchronized with media and should include dialogue plus relevant non-speech audio needed to understand the content. A transcript is a separate text representation that can support reading, searching, review, and access when synchronized playback is unnecessary. Source 2 explains captions, and Source 3 explains transcripts.

Audio description communicates visual information that is important for understanding but absent from the main audio, such as meaningful actions, changes of scene, or information shown only on screen. Source 4 explains this purpose. A transcript of dialogue alone does not replace missing visual information.

Alternatives require review for equivalence. Compare the spoken response, displayed text, captions, transcript, and visual presentation to check that they communicate the same instructions, warnings, choices, and corrections. Also test timing, speaker identification, reading order, control labels, focus movement, and operation without voice.

Do not assume that one alternative serves every learner. Include people who use the relevant access methods in evaluation, document barriers they encounter, and revise both the main interaction and its alternatives.

sections.title: Set privacy, safety, and role boundaries
paragraphs: Before collecting voice data, identify what is captured, why it is needed, whether derived text is retained, who can access it, how long it is retained, and how a learner can request correction or deletion where applicable. Exact legal duties and retention periods are UNKNOWN without a stated jurisdiction and organizational policy, so this module does not prescribe them.

Make the system's role clear. Learners should be able to distinguish an automated instructor from a person and should know when a person will review their interaction. Avoid implying expertise or authority that the system has not been assigned and evaluated to provide.

Risk decisions should consider the context, affected people, severity of a possible error, and ability to detect and recover from that error. Source 5 provides official guidance for managing risks associated with artificial intelligence systems.

Define escalation triggers before testing. Examples include repeated inability to understand the learner, a request outside the instructional scope, inaccessible content, conflicting assessment evidence, or a potentially harmful response. The escalation route must lead somewhere real; a label without an available recipient is not a recovery mechanism.

sections.title: Evaluate performance, learning, and access separately
paragraphs: Use separate measures for interaction performance, instructional progress, accessibility, and safety. A system can recognize speech accurately yet teach poorly, or provide correct instruction through controls that some learners cannot operate.

Interaction measures can include task completion, turns requiring correction, abandoned sessions, response delay, successful use of fallback paths, and successful escalation. Instructional measures can compare performance on the stated objective before and after the interaction or examine whether the learner can independently complete the target task.

Accessibility evaluation should cover voice and non-voice input, readable response text, captions, transcripts, audio description where visual information matters, keyboard operation, correction of recognized text, and recovery without speech. Test complete scenarios rather than checking isolated components only.

Numerical acceptance thresholds are UNKNOWN because the supplied requirements do not establish a use context, learner population, risk tolerance, or performance baseline. Establish thresholds with representative users and stakeholders before release, then record failures by pipeline stage so revisions target the actual problem.

A release review should answer five questions: Can the learner complete the target task, can the learner demonstrate the intended knowledge or skill, can the experience be operated through an alternative to voice, can mistakes be detected and corrected, and can unresolved cases reach a person or another valid channel?

questions.prompt: Which design begins a virtual instructor with an instructional purpose rather than conversation for its own sake?
choices: Start with a measurable learning objective and define evidence of progress.
Start with an unrestricted conversation and decide the objective after release.
Measure only whether the spoken response sounds fluent.
Remove retry paths so every learner follows one route.
questions.explanation: The module says to begin with a measurable learning objective and define the evidence that would demonstrate progress.

questions.prompt: What should happen before a consequential action when the interpreted spoken request may be wrong?
choices: Proceed because spoken output sounds confident.
Confirm the interpreted request and offer a correction path.
Delete the learner's input without explanation.
Replace the learning objective with a different one.
questions.explanation: The interaction-pipeline section recommends confirmation and correction when a mistaken interpretation could materially affect the learner.

questions.prompt: Which media alternative communicates important visual information that is absent from the main audio?
choices: Audio description
Speech recognition
Input confirmation
Dialogue management
questions.explanation: The accessible-media section defines audio description as communication of important visual information not conveyed by the main audio.

questions.prompt: Why should interaction performance and instructional progress be measured separately?
choices: A system may handle speech accurately while failing to help learners achieve the objective.
Instructional progress can always be inferred from response speed.
Accurate speech recognition proves that an answer is educationally correct.
Separate measures remove the need for accessibility evaluation.
questions.explanation: The module explains that successful speech handling does not establish successful teaching, so each outcome requires its own evidence.

questions.prompt: Which option is a valid recovery path after repeated speech-recognition difficulty?
choices: Offer editable recognized text or a text-input route.
Hide the recognized input from the learner.
Continue using the same interpretation without confirmation.
Declare that the learner completed the objective.
questions.explanation: The module identifies editable recognized text and switching to text input as recovery paths.

questions.prompt: What does the module say about numerical acceptance thresholds?
choices: They are UNKNOWN until the use context, learner population, risk tolerance, and baseline are established.
One universal threshold applies to every voice and learning context.
Thresholds are unnecessary if the response is fluent.
Thresholds should be selected without representative users.
questions.explanation: The evaluation section marks numerical thresholds UNKNOWN because the necessary contextual evidence was not supplied.

sections.title: Core terms
paragraphs: Model: a system that generates or evaluates outputs from learned patterns and current input.
Prompt: instructions and context supplied to a model.
Context window: the limited working material available for one interaction.
Agent: a model-driven system that can select tools and act in a loop.
Evaluation: a repeatable method for measuring output against explicit criteria.

resources.title: Daily AI Task Starter
resources.summary: A reusable prompt and working loop for turning ordinary work into a clear, verifiable AI task.

sections.title: Start with a useful contract
paragraphs: Replace each bracketed field with concrete information. Delete fields that do not apply instead of leaving placeholders for the model to guess.
For factual work, name the source of truth. For consequential work, include the required verification before accepting the result.

code.label: Copyable daily task prompt
code.code:
Outcome: [WHAT I NEED]
Audience: [WHO WILL USE IT]
Trusted context: [FACTS, FILES, OR LINKS]
Constraints: [MUST, MUST NOT, SCOPE]
Deliverable: [FORMAT AND LEVEL OF DETAIL]
Verify: [HOW TO CHECK THE RESULT]
Stop when: [DEFINITION OF DONE]

sections.title: Work in a short evidence loop
paragraphs: Ask for a first complete attempt, inspect the result against the stated outcome, then correct the missing context or constraint. Save the improved instruction when the task will recur.
Do not ask for endless polishing. Stop when the acceptance evidence passes or when a named uncertainty needs a person, a source, or a different tool.
sections.callout: A reusable prompt improves when you fix the instruction that caused the miss, not only the current output.

resources.title: Context Budget Playbook
resources.summary: Keep long AI sessions focused by loading the smallest useful working set and refreshing stale context deliberately.

sections.title: Build a working set, not a document pile
paragraphs: Give the model the instructions, source material, examples, and current state needed for the next decision. Large unrelated attachments compete for attention and make it harder to identify the source of truth.
Summarize stable decisions separately from raw exploration. Keep exact source text only when wording, code, or evidence must remain precise.

sections.title: Refresh when history becomes stale
paragraphs: Long sessions accumulate rejected ideas, superseded requirements, and tool output. Create a short handoff containing the goal, decisions, current state, verification, and next action before starting a clean session.
Do not compress away unresolved risks or user feedback. A useful handoff preserves why a decision was made, not only the final choice.

code.label: Clean-session handoff
code.code:
Goal: [CURRENT OUTCOME]
Decisions: [CHOICES AND WHY]
Current state: [WHAT EXISTS NOW]
Verified: [CHECKS THAT PASSED]
Open risks: [UNCERTAINTY TO PRESERVE]
Next action: [ONE CONCRETE STEP]

resources.title: AI Output Verification Ladder
resources.summary: Choose a level of checking that matches the claim, uncertainty, and consequence of the work.

sections.title: Match the check to the consequence
paragraphs: Low consequence: read for usefulness, internal consistency, and obvious mistakes.
Moderate consequence: compare against the supplied source, run examples or tests, and inspect edge cases.
High consequence: use current authoritative sources, independent review, domain expertise, and direct evidence from the real system.

sections.title: Ask what the evidence actually proves
paragraphs: A citation proves only what its source supports. A passing unit test proves only the behavior covered by that test. A successful deployment proves only that deployment completed.
Before accepting a broad claim, list its smaller claims and attach the nearest practical evidence to each one.
sections.callout: Fluency, confidence, and a successful tool call are signals. None is a substitute for evidence.
